issues.summary: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1s) like Ozempic can help with weight loss, which may assist with sleep apnea symptoms. If your sleep apnea has worsened with weight gain or you have other medical conditions that warrant the use of GLP-1s, your healthcare provider may prescribe one, but they can be pricey. Monthly out of pocket […] The post Will Insurance Cover Ozempic for Sleep Apne
issues.author: melissa
issues.content_html:
• How Does Ozempic Work for Sleep Apnea?
  • Is Ozempic Approved for Sleep Apnea?
  • Will Insurance Cover Ozempic for Sleep Apnea?
  • How to Check Your Insurance Coverage
  • Alternatives if Insurance Won’t Cover Ozempic
  • Frequently Asked Questions
Key Takeaways
  • Most insurance plans don’t cover Ozempic for sleep apnea, but some partially cover costs of another GLP-1, Zepbound, that’s prescribed for sleep apnea.
  • In 2024, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved Zepbound for the treatment of moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) in adults with obesity. Currently, Ozempic is only approved to treat type 2 diabetes.
  • You can find out if your insurance covers weight loss medications for sleep apnea by checking their online directory or calling your insurer directly.

Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1s) like Ozempic can help with weight loss, which may assist with sleep apnea symptoms. If your sleep apnea has worsened with weight gain or you have other medical conditions that warrant the use of GLP-1s, your healthcare provider may prescribe one, Trusted Source National Association of Insurance Commissioners View Source but they can be pricey. Monthly out of pocket costs often reach several hundred dollars, and some plans require you to try CPAP or a weight-loss program before approving the medication.

So, will insurance cover Ozempic for sleep apnea? The short answer is no, but some insurance plans may cover other GLP-1s for sleep apnea, especially if you also have other health conditions like high blood pressure or diabetes.

Even if your insurance won’t cover a GLP-1, you still have options. Your provider can document medical necessity, which strengthens insurance approval attempts for weight loss medications. Below, learn how weight loss drugs may improve sleep apnea, how to check your insurance coverage, and what other options exist.

Get a Home Sleep Study for as Low as $0

Based on claims data, eligible insured patients may pay as little as $0 for the home sleep study and related consultations. Actual out-of-pocket costs vary by insurance plan, deductible, coinsurance, and coverage. We will provide your out-of-pocket cost prior to your first consultation. Cost does not include any post-diagnosis medication or treatment, if and when prescribed.

Take a one-night sleep study in your own bed, review results with a certified sleep expert, and get a personalized treatment plan for as low $0 with most major insurance plans.

Check Your Coverage 4.8 60,000+ patients

How Does Ozempic Work for Sleep Apnea?

Obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) happens when your airway gets blocked during sleep, causing a pause in breathing. These episodes can happen many times throughout the night and last anywhere from 10 to 30 seconds.

Carrying extra weight around the neck is a major risk factor for OSA, as excess tissue can crowd your airway while you sleep Trusted Source MSD Manuals First published in 1899 as a small reference book for physicians and pharmacists, the Manual grew in size and scope to become one of the most widely used comprehensive medical resources for professionals and consumers. View Source . About 31% of people with obstructive sleep apnea have obesity while 44% are overweight Trusted Source National Library of Medicine, Biotech Information The National Center for Biotechnology Information advances science and health by providing access to biomedical and genomic information. View Source . Because of this connection, experts have started researching to see if GLP-1s like Ozempic can also improve symptoms of OSA Trusted Source Journal of Translational Medicine View Source .

A clear relationship exists between weight loss and better sleep apnea outcomes. A study review found that a 20% decrease in BMI led to a 57% reduction in sleep apnea symptoms Trusted Source National Library of Medicine, Biotech Information The National Center for Biotechnology Information advances science and health by providing access to biomedical and genomic information. View Source .

Other research confirms GLP-1s may improve sleep apnea symptoms through weight loss, a lower BMI (body mass index), and a smaller waist size. But not all GLP-1s offer the same benefits. For example, another study review found that tirzepatide (Zepbound) improved OSA symptoms more than liraglutide (Saxenda). Trials also show that tirzepatide improves daytime sleepiness and blood pressure, two issues that often accompany sleep apnea.

Is Ozempic Approved for Sleep Apnea?

Currently, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has not approved Ozempic to treat sleep apnea or weight loss. Ozempic is only approved by the FDA to treat type 2 diabetes. The only FDA-approved GLP-1s for weight loss are semaglutide (Wegovy), liraglutide (Saxenda), and tirzepatide (Zepbound).

Among these, only Zepbound has FDA approval for sleep apnea. In 2024, the FDA approved Zepbound for the treatment of moderate to severe OSA in adults with obesity Trusted Source U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) The FDA is responsible for protecting the public health by ensuring the safety, efficacy, and security of human and veterinary drugs, biological products, and medical devices; and by ensuring the safety of our nation's food supply, cosmetics, and products that emit radiation. View Source . This approval was based on a large clinical trial showing significant reductions in apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) or sleep apnea severity after weight loss.

Will Insurance Cover Ozempic for Sleep Apnea?

Insurance typically won’t cover Ozempic for sleep apnea since the FDA hasn’t approved its use for that condition. Sometimes, providers will prescribe medications “off-label,” meaning they offer them because they may help with a condition not listed in the approved indications. But insurers typically won’t cover a drug for off-label use.

However, if you have another health condition alongside OSA, you may still be eligible for GLP-1 coverage. For example, Ozempic is FDA-approved for type 2 diabetes, so if you have this condition, your insurance may pay for it. Weight loss and improved sleep apnea become added benefits. Trusted Source National Association of Insurance Commissioners View Source .

Some insurance plans also cover GLP-1s for obesity-related health conditions like high cholesterol or high blood pressure, but each company sets its own criteria. If you have one of these health conditions plus a high BMI and obstructive sleep apnea, you may get insurance coverage for GLP-1s.

Now that Zepbound has been approved to treat OSA, more insurers may cover this medication. Many payers are adding Zepbound to formularies, although prior authorization is common. Requirements often include a BMI threshold, documentation of CPAP intolerance or failure, and proof of structured weight loss attempts.

How to Check Your Insurance Coverage

Every insurance company has a range of coverage plans and each covers different drugs. The first place you can look is your insurance provider’s website. Most insurers have a formulary listed under each of their plans, so you can see exactly what’s covered and how much you can expect to pay.

Medicare and Medicaid have a similar list available online. If your insurance company’s online formulary is confusing or difficult to use, you can call the customer service number on the back of your insurance card to ask for copay information on any medication.

You can also submit an appeal if your provider submits a GLP-1 request for approval and insurance says they won’t pay. Appeals can push insurers a little harder if they have denied payment for your weight loss drug or if it’s not on their list of approved medications. You may be able to get it covered with an appeal if your provider can prove it’s medically necessary.

For most plans, you have six months to file an internal appeal with your insurer. If that appeal is denied, you can request an external review for a third-party to weigh in. Typically, appeals are submitted through your insurer’s website, but you may also request more information through their customer service.

Alternatives if Insurance Won’t Cover Ozempic

If your insurance plan won’t pay for Ozempic, you can ask about Zepbound or another GLP-1 medication. If no weight loss medication is covered, you still have options. Exercise and diet changes are encouraged for people on GLP-1s, and these changes improve sleep apnea symptoms on their own Trusted Source UpToDate More than 2 million healthcare providers around the world choose UpToDate to help make appropriate care decisions and drive better health outcomes. UpToDate delivers evidence-based clinical decision support that is clear, actionable, and rich with real-world insights. View Source .

To lose weight through diet, create a calorie deficit: take in fewer calories than you use daily. Trusted Source National Library of Medicine, Biotech Information The National Center for Biotechnology Information advances science and health by providing access to biomedical and genomic information. View Source .

Cutting foods like sweet and alcoholic beverages, may also help you lose weight faster. However, everyone responds differently to diets, so you may need to try more than one approach. Trusted Source National Library of Medicine, Biotech Information The National Center for Biotechnology Information advances science and health by providing access to biomedical and genomic information. View Source . You should also talk to your doctor before making any big lifestyle changes, especially because they may be able to make medically-sound suggestions based on your history or refer you to a nutritionist.

You can also boost your calorie deficit by exercising.. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services recommends getting 150 to 300 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise or 75 to 150 minutes of vigorous exercise each week. They also suggest you include muscle strengthening exercises at least two days per week . Adding resistance training is especially helpful because increased muscle mass improves metabolic rate.

Beyond lifestyle changes, your provider can recommend sleep apnea treatments like Trusted Source MSD Manuals First published in 1899 as a small reference book for physicians and pharmacists, the Manual grew in size and scope to become one of the most widely used comprehensive medical resources for professionals and consumers. View Source :

  • CPAP (continuous positive airway pressure) therapy, which keeps your airways open while you sleep.
  • Oral appliances that reposition or retrain your tongue to stay clear of your airway and prevent blockage.
  • Surgical options like nerve stimulation, tonsil removal, and excess tissue removal to improve OSA symptoms through a variety of methods.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does Medicare cover Ozempic for sleep apnea?

Medicare does not cover Ozempic for sleep apnea, but partially covers another GLP-1, Zepbound, for this diagnosis. Under Medicare, patients are expected to pay $50 per month for Zepbound.

How much is Ozempic without insurance?

Ozempic costs $499 per month without insurance. Some pharmacies offer discount programs, but costs still remain high.

How much is Ozempic with insurance?

The cost of Ozempic with insurance depends on your plan, but you may pay as little as $25 per month on some plans. To get a better idea of how much Ozempic can cost with your insurance plan, you can contact a representative from your insurance network to talk through any out-of-pocket costs.

How long will insurance cover Ozempic for sleep apnea?

The length of Ozempic coverage depends on your plan and health history. Typically, an initial authorization lasts for six months, but some plans cover this medication for 12 months at a time [/ocm_reference] . Renewals often require documented weight loss progress or updated provider notes.

issues.title: Selling to friends
issues.summary: There are two versions, very different: FAVOR: This is what multi-level marketing preys on. You ask a family member or a friend to buy something, not because they need it, but because you do. This doesn’t always end well. Someone might want to further their relationship with you by doing you this favor, but if […]
issues.author: Seth Godin
issues.content_html:
There are two versions, very different:

FAVOR: This is what multi-level marketing preys on. You ask a family member or a friend to buy something, not because they need it, but because you do.

This doesn’t always end well. Someone might want to further their relationship with you by doing you this favor, but if the unspoken promise is that the item or service is worthwhile, the disappointment that ensues hurts everyone. Real estate brokers or middlemen in a bind often seek to build friendly relationships at the club or community meetings, but then try to leverage this friendship into a significant sale without doing the hard work of actually being the best choice.

TRUST: This is the sort of sale that happens when you begin with the benefit of the doubt but actually deliver a great outcome. You’ll know this is the case when the person who trusted you ends up testifying on your behalf to others.

“No pressure” is something that’s showing up more and more in the pitches I’m seeing. Of course, there’s no pressure! Just saying it implies that you wish there were.

If you’re asking for a favor, you’re not serving and you’re not selling. You’re trading.

And if you’re asking for trust, be prepared to honor the obligation it creates.

issues.title: Practical empathy
issues.summary: I don’t know what you know. I don’t want what you want, see what you see, believe what you believe. And that’s okay. In fact, it’s the only way to be of service, to make a sale or to cause a change to happen. Of course, we’re more intimate with our ideas, our products and […]
issues.author: Seth Godin
issues.content_html:
I don’t know what you know. I don’t want what you want, see what you see, believe what you believe.

And that’s okay.

In fact, it’s the only way to be of service, to make a sale or to cause a change to happen.

Of course, we’re more intimate with our ideas, our products and our approach than anyone else. We have a noise in our head, a narrative and a point of view we’ve spent our whole lives creating. It’s naive to believe that anyone else is completely in sync with us.

And so, our only opportunity is to go where they are, not to demand that they come to us.

Practical empathy isn’t primarily an act of kindness (though it’s an essential component of kindness.) Instead, it’s a direct and straightforward path from here to there. It’s how we create action, learning and change.

Marketing is the simple and brave act of going to where someone else might be, and helping them get to where they hope to go.

issues.title: Confusion about causation
issues.summary: It’s not difficult to develop an incorrect theory. Ice cream and spaghetti have more letters than tofu and celery, so therefore, foods with long names are more fattening than those with short ones. If you start moving forward with this theory, you’ll soon find outliers. Sugar only has five letters, and watercress has ten. If […]
issues.author: Seth Godin
issues.content_html:
It’s not difficult to develop an incorrect theory. Ice cream and spaghetti have more letters than tofu and celery, so therefore, foods with long names are more fattening than those with short ones.

If you start moving forward with this theory, you’ll soon find outliers. Sugar only has five letters, and watercress has ten. If we want to stick with our theory, we’ll have to come up with more and more complex reasons why we ignore some of the data and embrace the rest.

Of course, this is absurd.

And yet we do it all the time. Ornate explanations about the stock market, SEO or politics. Charts and graphs where we spend most of our time fitting a plot to a few dots, or amplifying the obscure to justify the theory.

A simple theory that matches the data is much more likely to accurately explain causation. It might not be a comfortable theory, or one that matches our trajectory, but it’s a better theory.

It turns out that the number of letters is completely irrelevant to how fattening a food is. I’m sorry you spent all this time on research, but you’re on the wrong path.

If you want to know why your marketing, your investments or your arguments are floundering, it might pay to reconsider the theory, not look for more data to justify the current one.

issues.title: 5 Interesting Learnings from the Databricks AI Index: Open-Weight Jumps to 31% of Enterprise Tokens, 72% of Companies Now Use Multiple Model Providers, and a 281x Gap Between Median and Power Users
issues.summary: Most model share data we get comes from consumer apps, developer routers, or surveys. The Databricks AI Index uses a different source: actual token traffic from more than 10,000 companies that route their AI through Databricks’ Unity Gateway. That includes Fortune 500 and Global 2000 companies, plus traffic Databricks sends out to Anthropic and OpenAI.... Continue Reading
issues.author: Jason Lemkin
issues.content_html:
Most model share data we get comes from consumer apps, developer routers, or surveys. The Databricks AI Index uses a different source: actual token traffic from more than 10,000 companies that route their AI through Databricks’ Unity Gateway. That includes Fortune 500 and Global 2000 companies, plus traffic Databricks sends out to Anthropic and OpenAI.

One caveat before the data. Databricks hosts open-weight models and has a commercial interest in companies using them, so its customers probably lean further toward open-weight than the average enterprise. Even with that discount, the speed of what changed here is hard to ignore.

1. Open-Weight Went From 7.3% to 30.9% of Enterprise Tokens in About Four Months

Open-weight share of enterprise token traffic: 7.3% in July, 30.9% in November.

Patrick Wendell, a Databricks co-founder, said why in his launch thread. Anecdotally, companies use them mostly to cut costs on high-volume work. Enterprises are not swapping open-weight in for Claude on their hardest problems. They’re moving the bulk work there: classification, extraction, summarization, the stuff that runs a million times a day.

Two details stand out:

  • The open-weight leaders are mostly Chinese labs. The index lists Zhipu (GLM), DeepSeek, and Moonshot (Kimi) as the open-weight providers. These are large enterprises running Chinese-origin weights on US infrastructure, at volume. A year ago most enterprise security teams would have said no.
  • One model release can move the whole category. GLM 5.2 accounts for about 40% of open-weight tokens on the gateway, one month after its mid-July availability.

What this means if you’re building: If your product makes a model call on every record, every ticket, or every email, a third of your enterprise buyers’ traffic now runs on models that cost a fraction of frontier pricing. Your competitors will rebuild their COGS on open-weight. If you still route everything to a frontier model, you’ll lose on gross margin before you lose on product.

2. Single-Provider Companies Fell From 64% to 28%

Enterprises on Unity Gateway relying on one model provider: about 64% in July, falling to 28% by November 2. That happened in one quarter.

Databricks’ earlier data shows the same trend at the model level. Average unique models per customer rose from 4.2 to 7.1 since January. Roughly 40% of those models were open-weight.

Enterprises now treat models the way they treat cloud regions: several in use, routed by workload, swapped out when something better ships. It matters for two reasons:

  • “We’re built on GPT” or “we’re built on Claude” isn’t a moat, and enterprise buyers don’t want to hear it. They want to know you can use whichever model they’ve already approved, including the open-weight ones running inside their own perimeter.
  • The release pace makes lock-in impossible anyway. Since May 2026, a new flagship model launched roughly every week, or every 3.7 days when regional labs are included.

3. Anthropic Still Owns the Proprietary Side, and Opus 5.5 Took Over in Six Weeks

Open-weight is growing, but Anthropic’s lead within proprietary models grew too. Anthropic’s overall share rose from 57.6% to 68.8% over the period covered, which the article ties to Opus 5.5’s launch.

How fast it happened is the real point. Claude Opus 5.5 went from 7.2% to 37.9% of proprietary-model tokens in six weeks. Enterprises are supposed to be slow. These ones moved a third of their proprietary traffic to a new model in a month and a half, because a gateway turns switching into a config change.

The flip side matters just as much. The best model on Databricks’ coding benchmark is Claude Fable 5.1, yet Fable 5.1’s share of proprietary tokens fell from 5.5% to 0.6% over six weeks. The most capable model is not the most used. Once a model is good enough at a lower price, enterprises move to it.

Databricks did the same thing internally. They kept Opus 4.8 rather than upgrading to Opus 5, because the upgrade wasn’t worth the added cost for its workloads.

4. Gemini 3.8 Flash Had a Low Token Price and Cost $11.97 Per Task

This is the most useful section for anyone pricing an AI product. Databricks built a coding benchmark from real merged pull requests in its multi-million-line codebase and measured cost per task, not cost per token.

  • Best quality: Claude Fable 5.1 at 96.0% task success, $7.47 per task. Muse Wonder: 94.9% at $1.53 per task. That extra 1.1 points costs almost 5x as much.
  • GPT-6 Luna and Claude Opus 5.5 both hit 89.1%. Luna averaged $0.05 per task versus $1.62 for Opus 5.5, about 32x less.
  • Gemini 3.8 Flash averaged 140 turns per task and $11.97 per task, one of the most expensive in the benchmark despite a low token price.
  • On open-weight, DeepSeek V4.1 and GLM 5.3 are both third, with a 93.1% pass rate, which is ahead of Opus 5.5 on this benchmark.

The harness matters almost as much as the model. In a separate test, the same model scored 61.7% in one harness, 48.1% in another, and 38.4% bare.

The decision for founders: Stop judging models by price per million tokens. A cheap model that takes 140 turns to finish costs more than an expensive one that finishes in 10. Measure cost per completed task on your own workload. Same score, 32x cost difference. That’s your gross margin.

5. The Median User Spends $2.49 a Week. The P99 User Spends $699.74.

This is the number I’d put in front of every B2B CEO still pricing AI per seat.

Median: $2.49. It more than doubled from $1.10 over six weeks. P90: no value given. The article says it stayed “relatively flat.” P99: $699.74, about 281x the median.

$700 a week works out to about $36,000 a year in list-price tokens for one person. That’s more than most companies pay per seat for any software they own. And the median user doubled their spend in six weeks.

It means three things:

  • Flat per-seat pricing breaks at the top of the distribution. Your heaviest 1% of users can wipe out the margin from everyone else. You need usage caps, credits, or tiers that track consumption.
  • The budget is real, and it isn’t software budget. I’ve said I won’t invest in an agentic B2B company unless it unlocks budget beyond software budget. Paying $36K a year for one power user’s tokens is the clearest sign yet that this budget exists. It’s being spent on headcount-level output, not on seats.
  • CFOs are about to notice. Databricks titled one of its own posts “The AI Bill is coming.” Expect enterprise buyers to ask you for per-user budgets, routing, and visibility into spend before they’ll sign.

A Few More Interesting Learnings

  • Better models can cost less. Inside Databricks, Opus 5.5 delivered improved quality at 29% lower cost per session than its predecessor. Upgrading isn’t always a price increase.
  • Frontier guardrails are pushing some work to open-weight. Hosted frontier models refused Hugging Face responders’ analysis of attack logs and exploit payloads. The team used GLM 5.2 instead. Security and other edge-case workloads will move to models you can run yourself.
  • Data retention is now a selling point. Databricks says frontier providers have departed from zero-data-retention, including a 30-day minimum retention tied to Anthropic’s frontier tier. If you sell to regulated industries, expect retention terms to become part of model selection.
  • The #1 model keeps changing. The top intelligence ranking has changed hands 20+ times since May 2023. Build the routing layer now, because the model you depend on today won’t be the leader next quarter.
  • Wasted agent tokens are a large, hidden cost. One Databricks post describes cutting $1 million a year of wasted agent spend in one hour by fixing bugs in MCP tool servers. If you run agents in production and nobody is tracing tool calls, you’re probably paying for loops.

Sources:

  • Databricks AI Index
  • Introducing the Databricks AI Index (Databricks blog)
  • The Enterprise Case for Open-Weight Models (Databricks blog)
  • FourWeekMBA on Wendell’s launch thread

issues.title: How Fast Do You Really Have to Be Growing to Raise Venture Capital Today? $1M to $100M ARR in 5 Years, Max. But VCs Are Hoping for 2-3 Years
issues.summary: Of course, even faster is better 😉 A top topic with founders and VCs who have been around since the pre-AI era: is T2D3 dead? Is 100% growth … too low? Do I need to be an AI company? My simplification, stress-tested against both funds’ portfolios and the last two years of rounds I’ve seen:... Continue Reading
issues.author: Jason Lemkin
issues.content_html:
Of course, even faster is better 😉

A top topic with founders and VCs who have been around since the pre-AI era: is T2D3 dead ? Is 100% growth … too low? Do I need to be an AI company?

My simplification, stress-tested against both funds’ portfolios and the last two years of rounds I’ve seen:

You need to go from $1M to $100M ARR in 5 years or less to raise venture capital today. Faster is better.

Two things that rule does not say:

It doesn’t say you have to get to $1M ARR quickly. Early capital is patient. Seed is still priced on team, wedge, and early signal, and taking three years to find the thing is more or less fine.

And it doesn’t say growth is the only thing that matters. Retention, gross margin, and burn all still get diligenced hard. But they get diligenced after the growth rate clears the bar. They don’t substitute for it.

The clock starts at $1M ARR. From there you have five years.

"Let me summarize venture capital today:

All That Matters is Growth.

Do gross margins matter? No
Does it matter if revenue recurs? No
Does customer concentration matter? No" pic.twitter.com/7GxfOENRcb

— Jason ✨👾SaaStr.Ai✨ Lemkin (@jasonlk) September 30, 2026

What “$1M to $100M in 5 Years” Actually Requires

100x in five years is 151% growth a year, compounded, five years running.

Now put it next to T2D3, which Neeraj Agrawal coined at Battery a decade ago and which became the canonical venture growth path: triple, triple, double, double, double.

T2D3 is actually ahead through year 3, because tripling beats 151%. Then it falls behind and finishes at $72M, 28% short.

So T2D3 didn’t die. It got demoted. The aspirational path of 2016 is now roughly the minimum, and you have to beat it by a year or start the run at $1.4M instead of $1M.

Work Backward From the IPO and the Number Falls Out

Importantly, the growth bar isn’t realy set by VCs. It’s set by the exit, and every stage prices off it.

Sapphire Ventures’ 2026 Software x AI report puts the current IPO calculus at $400M to $500M+ in revenue, 20%+ growth at scale, positive free cash flow or a credible path to it, and an AI story that holds up. For a strong IPO, where the aftermarket works and the round you raised at is a floor rather than a ceiling, the real number is $500M+ growing 50%+.

Look at what actually cleared it. Figma priced its IPO in July 2025 at $33, valuing it around $19.3 billion, on $749M of 2024 revenue growing 48%, roughly $1B of ARR at listing, 91% gross margins, and Q1 2025 net income of $44.9M. It closed day one near $47 billion.

Then the market repriced it anyway . Figma’s first public quarter came in at 41% growth and the stock fell about 20% the next day. Profitable, $1B of revenue, growing 41%, and public investors took a fifth of the market cap off for the deceleration.

Now run the second ladder. If you hit $100M ARR in year 5 and hold 50% growth from there:

Nine years from $1M to $500M+ ARR still growing 50%. That’s the whole arc, and it only works if you clear the first checkpoint on time. Miss year 5 by two years and you arrive at $500M growing 30%, which is a fine business and a mediocre IPO.

The Multiples Did the Damage, Not the Growth Rates

The revenue bar went up mostly because the multiple went down.

Per Sapphire’s 2026 data, even the fastest growers, 25%+ revenue growth, now trade at 8.3x NTM revenue against a 10-year average of 10.8x. Public enterprise software has lost $2.4 trillion in market cap since the October 2025 peak. The Sapphire Broad Software Index is down 29% from peak and the Pure SaaS Index is down 30%. Unlike every prior 20%+ software drawdown since 2001, this one is not tracking a broader Nasdaq decline, which tells you it’s structural rather than macro.

Do the arithmetic on what that means for the exit. At 10.8x, a $400M-revenue company is worth $4.3B. At 8.3x it’s worth $3.3B. To get back to $4.3B you need $520M of revenue.

Every stage below the IPO reprices off that same number. Series C investors underwriting a $4B exit now need 30% more revenue at the exit than they did against the 10-year average multiple, and they push that requirement down to the B, and the B pushes it to the A.

The Fund Math at the Valuations Founders Are Raising At

Per Carta’s Q1 2026 data, the Series A bar for AI startups is now around $3.5M ARR, roughly 3.5x the ~$1M bar from three years ago, with the median AI Series A at $13M to $15M on a $75M to $250M post. Over 60 cents of every venture dollar Carta tracked in Q1 2026 went to AI companies.

So: a fund buys 15% to 20% at Series A on a nine-figure post. After the B, C, and D, that’s 7% to 10% at exit. For that position to return a real multiple on a $60M fund, the company has to be worth several billion dollars.

At 8x revenue, several billion dollars means $400M to $600M of revenue.

There is no version of this where the company gets there without going from $1M to $100M in about five years. The entry price already spent the optionality. And it binds the seed round too, because seed is underwritten against the same terminal number.

Entrata Filed With $509M of Revenue Growing 24%. It’s a PE Listing.

Entrata filed to go public with $509.3M of 2025 revenue, up from $412.0M, so 24% growth, cash-flow positive, with Q1 2026 revenue of $143.5M against $116.6M a year prior.

Over $500M of revenue, profitable, category leader in multifamily property management software. By any operating standard, an excellent company.

It’s also PE-owned, and it’s leading a wave of PE-owned software listings rather than venture-backed ones, because a buyout fund has a defined life and LPs counting distributions. A venture-backed company compounding at 40%+ can wait, raise privately, or run a continuation vehicle. Most sponsor-owned names can’t.

Meanwhile the venture-backed B2B software window has been effectively shut. As of May 2026 there were zero software listings against 32 total IPOs, and Renaissance Capital expects 200 to 230 IPOs across 2026 with sponsors leading the calendar.

So $500M of ARR by itself doesn’t clear the bar. $500M growing 50% clears it. And if the honest forecast is a $500M business growing 24%, the capital that fits is private equity or growth equity, which is a much cheaper thing to learn at $20M ARR than at $200M.

Entrata at $575m ARR Growing 23% Is First of the Next Wave of PE-Backed Software IPOs. The Catch: Almost None of Them Are Accelerating.

Cursor Went From $1M to $100M in 12 Months. That’s the Comp Now. It’s Crazy, But It’s an AI-Fueled World.

This bar has teeth in 2026 and didn’t in 2019 because the top of the market moved far enough to drag the reference point with it.

  • Cursor went from $1M to $100M ARR in roughly 12 months, then $300M three months later, $500M three months after that, $1B by November 2025 and $2B by February 2026.
  • Lovable hit $100M ARR in about eight months with 45 employees, and $400M by February 2026 with 146 people, roughly $2.77M of ARR per employee.
  • ElevenLabs went from $100M in January 2025 to $2B by February 2026.

The pattern holds below the outliers too. ICONIQ’s top-quartile companies under $50M ARR grew 111% in the second half of 2025. The median private B2B company grew 22%.

Venture rounds get priced against the first number, not the second. A company doing $8M ARR growing 40% beats the median of every private benchmark published this year and is still a hard venture fundraise. The business can be excellent. It’s the capital pool that doesn’t fit.

Where This Rule Breaks

I’d rather give you the exceptions than have you discover them in a board meeting.

Infrastructure and deeply technical categories get more time. If the product takes three years to build and the contracts are seven figures, sophisticated investors will underwrite a slower ramp to $100M against a much larger terminal number. Databricks and Snowflake did not run this curve.

Consumption businesses report revenue, not ARR, and the shapes differ. A usage-based company can look flat for three quarters and then step-function when one customer moves a workload into production. Applying an ARR rule to a consumption line item produces bad conclusions in both directions.

Retention can buy you a year. $12M ARR growing 55% with 135% NRR and a 12-month CAC payback is a fundable Series B in 2026. $12M growing 55% with 98% NRR is usually not. The growth bar and the retention bar trade against each other at the margin, though not by much and not for long.

The best argument against all of this: the 2021 vintage proved that pricing companies off a five-year 100x curve produces enormous markdowns when the curve breaks, and plenty of good investors think the right response to an 8.3x market is to underwrite slower, cheaper, more durable companies rather than to raise the growth bar. That view might win over the next decade. It just isn’t how most rounds are getting priced right now.

What to Do With This Before Your Next Round

If you’re under $1M ARR: ignore all of it. You have time, and the worst thing you can do is force growth before the wedge is real.

If you just crossed $1M: mark the date. Five years from that date, you need a $100M ARR business, and that means you need to know inside of 18 months whether the motion compounds at 150% or at 60%. Those are different companies with different capital structures, and both can be great.

If you’re at $10M to $30M growing 40% to 60%: you’re running the most common and most painful profile in B2B right now. Above the median, below the venture bar. The move is to pick your capital deliberately rather than spend nine months discovering the mismatch through 40 investor meetings. Growth equity, a strategic minority round, and staying default-alive on your own cash are all real answers.

And if you’re on the 151% curve: raise more than you think you need. Capital is concentrating hard, over 60 cents of every venture dollar went to AI in Q1, and the premium for actually being on the curve is the largest I’ve seen it.

Owner Did It With Restaurants ($1M to $100M in 5 Years), Fueled in Part By Going All-In on AI

issues.title: Dear SaaStr: How Many Of Our Prospects and Customers Should I Meet Face-to-Face?
issues.summary: Dear SaaStr: Should an early- stage B2B startup meet every customer face-to-face to receive feedback? If you could — all of them. The more customers you meet in person, the more that buy from you, and the more “more stuff” they buy from you after,. The full data here from Toast, Brex, Slice and more... Continue Reading
issues.author: Jason Lemkin
issues.content_html:
Dear SaaStr: Should an early- stage B2B startup meet every customer face-to-face to receive feedback?

If you could — all of them. The more customers you meet in person, the more that buy from you, and the more “more stuff” they buy from you after,.

The full data here from Toast, Brex, Slice and more here:

In-Person Sales Generate 3x Higher Conversions Per The CROs of Toast, Splunk, Brex and Slice

But if you don’t have a big enough team to do so, or the DNA yet, then as a rough rule, who should you take the time to go meet? Because it does take time. The answer really is — meet as many as you can in person.

But some rough rules to think about:

  • Meet every local customer that you can Uber/drive to in the early days … if they’ll take a meeting (a lot won’t want to). Try to meet every single of your first 100 customers in person that are local, no matter how small the deal size.
  • The more your product is a “solution” vs. just a tool — the more meetings you should take . To learn how your solution is really being used.
  • Meet with ALL your top 10, or top 10% customers . So if you have 50-70 today … if nothing else … meet in person with at least the Top 5 or so. It will dramatically increase the odds they deploy, expand, and stay. Customers love to meet with the CEO. You owe it at least to your top customers.
  • If nothing else, try to spend 20% of your time with your existing customers . Everyone spends too much time on prospects, and not enough time with closed customers.

Having said all that, what’s clearly changed is when you meet your prospects and customers in the funnel.

With Zoom as the default, and AI now doing the research, the notes, and half the follow-up, the face-to-faces in most cases are later in the sales (and VC) funnel. Founders don’t meet with VCs for a first meeting: they meet for a penultimate meeting. And in sales, folks are less and less likely now to fly out for an initial meeting, and more likely to fly out for a meeting further down the funnel.

And honestly, that makes the in-person meeting worth more, not less. Everything async is basically free now. The meeting in the room is the part AI can’t do for you: trust, reading the room, and getting the real answer.

But it hasn’t changed how important it is to meet face-to-face with your top prospects and customers. It’s just changed a little bit when you do.

And if you’ve been a bit slow to get to back to that, to those IRL meetings, well it’s time. Because your competitors are.

Finally, we did an analysis across about 240+ of our sponsors at SaaStr itself. Net net, we closed 42% more revenue from sponsors we met IRL.

That included upsells, churn, and deal size. One little case study, but there you go.

More here: SaaStr | Want Happy Customers? Implement the 5-Visits-Plus-2-Badges Rule. For Your Customer Success Team — And You.

Customers Love to Talk to the CEO. Do More of That.

issues.title: Dear SaaStr: What Was the Toughest Rejection You Ever Had in Sales?
issues.summary: Dear SaaStr: What Was the Toughest Rejection You Ever Had in Sales? The hardest rejection I’ve had in sales was around renewals. Especially ones I thought we really had earned. But still lost. In particular, in the early days of EchoSign / Adobe Sign, we had a particular manager at a strategic partner where I... Continue Reading
issues.author: Jason Lemkin
issues.content_html:
Dear SaaStr: What Was the Toughest Rejection You Ever Had in Sales?

The hardest rejection I’ve had in sales was around renewals. Especially ones I thought we really had earned. But still lost.

In particular, in the early days of EchoSign / Adobe Sign, we had a particular manager at a strategic partner where I did everything I could to help him. We made nothing off this partner — zilch — but I did everything I could to help him succeed. I built an integration when no one else would. I even flew to an event to help him, again for $0. He also had been to our home personally. A coincidence, but someone who I’d broken bread with on several levels and in several states.

He then joined one of our top logo customers as a manager. The next week, he called to tell us he was canceling the contract. We’d just done an NPS survey and found the team he had just inherited loved us. 100% support. Zero complaints. It was a game-changer for them. And no one there was asking for change management to learn a new vendor.

But … our competition was smart. They’d essentially bribed him. They’d already wined and dined him before he even started. They’d offered to do case studies with him and invited him already to their VIP Customer Conference. They’d also already invited him to a retreat in Napa. They’d offered to make him a hero. And he really didn’t care about the costs to switch vendors, or which one was better for his new team.

We lost this top logo customer, despite making everyone there insanely happy.

It hurt.

Champion change is tough. It’s risky. And when it comes, you gotta jump on it. If you don’t — the competition will.

And remember, go long. More times that not, you’ll get another chance if you treat a happy customer that churns well. It just may be years down the road.

More here: Champion Change: You Gotta Jump On It | SaaStr

issues.title: How to track your brand's visibility in AI search [2026]

In 2025, nearly a third of Gen Z consumers (31%) defaulted to chatbots or AI to find information online, according to HubSpot’s 2025 AI Trends for Marketers report , and it’s clear that AI search i
issues.author: Zoe Ashbridge
issues.content_html:
Marketers need to know how to track brand visibility in AI search because search has changed. AI-generated answers now show up earlier in the discovery journey, often before a traditional search result. In 2025, nearly a third of Gen Z consumers (31%) defaulted to chatbots or AI to find information online, according to HubSpot’s 2025 AI Trends for Marketers report, and it’s clear that AI search is growing — rapidly. In 2026, Google reported that AI Mode has over one billion monthly users, and queries have doubled every quarter since launch.

Failure to place brands in AI Overviews (AIO) or within AI search tools like ChatGPT, Perplexity, or Claude is a failure to meet prospective buyers where they’re searching. That’s harmful to audience connection, conversion, and ultimately, revenue. Brands that show up in AI search are the ones that audiences consider. The ones that don’t simply disappear from the conversation, with no ranking position, no impression count, and no obvious way to tell.

This article breaks down what brand visibility is, how to track brand visibility in AI search, the Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) that marketers need to pay attention to, and the best tools to support AI visibility tracking.

Table of Contents

  • What is AI search and brand visibility?
  • How to Track Brand Visibility in AI Search Right Now.
  • How to Track Brand Visibility in AI Search with the Right KPIs and Cadence
  • How to Track Brand Visibility in AI Search with a Repeatable System
  • How to Improve AI Search Visibility and Fix Inaccurate Answers
  • Best Tools to Track Brand Visibility In AI Search
  • How To Connect AI Visibility To Content And Pipeline
  • Frequently Asked Questions About Tracking AI Search Visibility
  • Tracking AI visibility isn’t optional anymore — search changed.

What is AI search and brand visibility?

AI search refers to search that takes place on AI platforms, like ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google Gemini, Microsoft Copilot, and Google’s AI Overviews. There are many more, and AI search platforms are growing. Unlike Google or other search engines, which return a list of links to click through, AI search engines answer questions directly. Those answers are lifted or paraphrased from trusted sources.

Brand visibility in AI search relates to the impressions that brands get within AI platforms. A brand mentioned or cited in AI in an answer has visibility. Brand visibility in AI search includes mentions, citations, sentiment, and accuracy. The goal is for brands to increase their visibility. They want to be cited and mentioned often, accurately, and favorably.

How to Track Brand Visibility in AI Search Right Now

The most basic way to check AI brand visibility is manually: Open ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, and Copilot. Ask the same set of questions across each one. Then, record whether the brand appears, how it’s described, and whether competitors show up instead. This is an easy starting point. But, it breaks down quickly.

A single spot check only captures one moment in time. That result reflects one user’s search history and personalization, not any broader trend. When multiplied across several platforms and hundreds to thousands of prompt variations, manual tracking becomes a task that nobody has time to maintain.

HubSpot ran an experiment testing hundreds of queries across AI chatbots, search engines, and social platforms. The experiment found that AI tools were noticeably weaker at handling specific, niche information, like details about a particular local business, than they were at answering broad or general questions. This is why prompts need to be tracked consistently — and ideally automatically. No one can infer how a platform or brand performs across the board just because it performs well in one prompt, particularly if that prompt is broad and general.

This is where dedicated tools come in.

Rather than replaying the same prompts by hand, tools built for AI brand tracking run them automatically, on a schedule, across multiple engines at once, then organize the results into a usable format, such as:

  • Which prompts triggered a mention.
  • Which sources got cited.
  • How sentiment trended over time.

Different tools approach brand visibility measurement in different ways; some focus narrowly on mention frequency, others build out fuller scoring models across multiple dimensions.

HubSpot’s free AI Search Grader is one example. The grader gives marketers a baseline read on AI visibility, and what it provides for free is pretty amazing. Here’s what the start of the report looks like.

While tools like AI Search Grader are excellent, there are limitations.

AI Search Grader captures a baseline read; it doesn’t track improvements or declines in trends. Ideally, most marketing teams will move from a one-time snapshot to ongoing tracking, so that they can adapt marketing strategy based on data.

Tools like HubSpot AEO provide ongoing tracking and data related to performance in AI search tools. It monitors brand mentions, citations, and sentiment across AI platforms continuously. With continuous tracking, marketing teams can see how efforts and campaigns have impacted visibility.

Here’s a look at a citations report, showing a brand’s domain performance versus competitors:

How to Track Brand Visibility in AI Search with the Right KPIs and Cadence

Switching between tools or KPIs will only provide inconsistent and confusing results. No two tools report the same numbers. All a tool can provide is a third-party overview of what’s happening with a brand’s visibility, and none of them are completely accurate.

Feedback from a tool should be treated as a directive, not absolute truth. What marketers are looking for are trends in the data, and that comes from consistent tracking using the same tool and the same metrics.

Now that caveat is out there, let’s look at KPIs:

Brand Mention Rate

Brand mention rate measures how often a brand appears in AI-generated answers. It’s a foundational metric; it’s calculated by dividing the number of AI answers that mention the brand by the total number of answers analyzed across a set of tracked prompts. A low mention rate indicates that AI platforms rarely surface the brand at all.

Here’s an example of a brand mention in ChatGPT. The mention of the brand is there, but there’s no clickable link:

Mentions and citations are not the same thing: an AI platform might mention a brand by name without linking to anything it owns, or it might cite a third-party review site instead of the brand’s own content.

Citation Rate

Citation rate measures how often AI answers link to or reference brand-owned sources. Tracking citation rates separately shows which domains and pages are actually earning a reference inside AI answers, which points directly to the content that needs to be built or strengthened.

Here’s an example of a brand citation in AIO. There’s an actual link, and if clicked, the user will visit the website of the cited source (in this case, HubSpot):

Source

Pro tip: To support citation rates, marketers can track actual clicks to the website from AI sources. I include this metric on all of my client reports. It reports to stakeholders that we’re getting cited, but also that these citations are turning into valuable actions for the business. Kyle Rushton-McGregor has a guide on how to track AI visits in GA4.

Sentiment and Accuracy

Sentiment measures how AI platforms describe a brand. It’s typically scored on a scale from negative to positive.

Accuracy is related to sentiment.

Marketers want their brands to appear accurately in AI.

A negative sentiment might not be a bad thing if it’s accurate. For example, if an AI platform describes a brand as ‘expensive compared to competitors’ and that brand has a premium price point, the sentiment reads as negative, but the description is accurate, and the brand probably wants to defer searchers looking for a cheap solution.

That said, marketers must manage brand sentiment and ensure that sentiment is overall positive. Brand sentiment can teach marketers about things customers are unhappy about. If marketing comes across a repeated negative sentiment, then they can share information with customer success or product development to try to change that narrative.

Share of Voice

Share of voice measures how often AI search platforms mention a brand compared to competitors across the same set of prompts. It’s important because if marketers look at their brand in isolation, the mention rate might look great, but comparing share of voice against competitors reveals the wider opportunities and potential.

A low share of voice relative to competitors shows where the gaps are and what brands need to do to close the gap.

How to Track Brand Visibility in AI Search with a Repeatable System

A repeatable system turns AI brand tracking from ad hoc checks into a data-driven marketing approach. With this approach, marketing teams can make strategic decisions based on data and trends, leading them to meaningful solutions that improve a brand’s visibility in AI search.

The following five steps give marketing and AEO (also called GEO) teams a framework to set up once and run on an ongoing basis.

1. Run a baseline visibility check.

Before setting up ongoing tracking, it helps to research and establish a starting point. Otherwise, marketing is creating a tracking system based mostly on feeling.

AI Search Grader helps measure brand visibility in AI search, scoring how ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity currently describe a brand across sentiment, presence quality, brand recognition, share of voice, and market position.

Marketers can use tools like AI Search Grader to get a big-picture overview of how their brand performs. They’ll start to build a picture of how the brand sentiment looks and where there might be opportunities.

And it’s free. So, marketing can run AI Search Grader for competitors to build a mental map of the wider AI search landscape. The beauty of AI Search Grader is that there are no limits, so marketing teams can use this free tool as much as they like. Every search in AI Search Grader builds research, curiosity, and insights that can be carried into the final plan.

2. Write consistent, structured prompts.

AI search tracking requires consistent prompts across multiple AI platforms. Like switching tools or KPIs, switching prompt wording between checks makes it impossible to tell whether a shift in results reflects a change in visibility or just a different question.

Marketing teams should write out the exact prompt list in advance, document it, and reuse the same wording every time a check runs. This is a lot easier when working with a tool, because the tools will categorize prompts and maintain the exact prompt over time, but if working manually, marketers need to manage it.

Tools like AI Search Grader can inspire prompt selection, but marketers don’t have to stop there. Existing keyword research is a great starting point, especially long-tail keywords in Google Search Console (GSC). Specifically, keywords that include problems and solutions for certain audiences, for example, “How do I solve [problem] in my [company]” or “how to fix [problem] in your forties.” Many keywords are already phrased as questions, or close enough that it’s not a leap to see how they’d translate into a query on an AI platform.

Talking directly to customers helps, too. Sales and customer success teams often have a good sense of the exact language prospects use when researching a purchase. If sales or customer support have a good relationship, they could even ask customers if they’d share their own AI chat history, which will surface real prompts marketing teams would not have thought to write themselves.

Important note: Asking for chat history could be invasive. This ask can only work if there’s a customer relationship that’s already been built.

Once marketing has the prompts locked down, it’s time to decide where to track them and how to manage them.

3. Map the core AI platforms and build a prompt taxonomy.

Core AI platforms include ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, Copilot, and Google AI Overviews. However, most brands don’t need to track every single platform, which is good news for brands working with tighter budgets. Some tools charge a base fee for ChatGPT tracking, with add-on costs for each additional AI platform.

How to Decide Which Platforms to Track

For one of my clients, who had a limited budget, we focused solely on ChatGPT. We used a marketing report to decide which platforms to pay the most attention to. I tracked clicks from all the core platforms, as well as a few others. Clicks from ChatGPT far exceeded all other core AI platforms, with over 87.18% of total AI visits coming from ChatGPT. Claude and Gemini were next with 4.49% each, then Copilot at 2.56% and Perplexity at 1.28%.

Important note: Some AEO tools don’t charge to track data from additional AI tools, so check what the tools allow users to track as part of a free or paid package, and what costs extra.

HubSpot’s AEO tracks brand visibility across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity as part of the same $50-a-month package, with no extra charge to add the second or third platform once a prompt allowance is purchased. Other tools, like Profound.ai, charge $99/month to track ChatGPT, then $399/month to track three platforms.

For my client, HubSpot AEO is ideal because it’s affordable and tracks the major AI platform they need — ChatGPT.

Once marketing has the platforms to track, marketers need a prompt taxonomy (a way of organizing prompts). The prompt taxonomy should include brand, competitor, category, task-based, and comparison prompts.

Check out the example below.

4. Set a tracking cadence and automate ongoing monitoring.

With prompts written, categorized, and platforms selected, the last piece is deciding how often to check them.

Cadence matters as much as the metrics themselves. Weekly reviews support baseline AI brand monitoring, giving marketing and SEO teams a steady read on trends without demanding daily attention. Daily checks make sense during active optimization sprints — testing content changes, responding to a citation gap, or catching a sentiment issue that needs a fast fix.

Tools like HubSpot AEO automate this cadence, running the same prompt set across engines on a schedule and organizing the results so nobody has to manually replay the same questions week after week.

5. Route visibility data into CRM and content workflows.

If marketing can route visibility data into CRM and content workflows, AI visibility can turn from a vanity metric into a revenue input. With this, AI reporting becomes highly engaging to stakeholders, who ultimately care about revenue because it shows how AI search performance and pipeline are integrated.

This ‌routing is where most standalone AEO tools fall short entirely. The fact that HubSpot AEO is built on a CRM gives it an incredible advantage.

With an integrated CRM and AI tool, visibility data becomes a system where it gets routed to the people and workflows that can respond to it.

Here’s how:

  • HubSpot Smart CRM stores AI visibility properties, prompt clusters, and dashboard data, keeping visibility metrics in the same system as the rest of a brand’s customer and campaign data instead of siloed in a separate tool.
  • HubSpot Content Hub turns visibility gaps into content briefs and refreshes, so a low mention rate on a topic becomes an assignment rather than a stat that nobody acts on.
  • HubSpot Marketing Hub connects AI visibility efforts to campaign reporting and attribution, closing the loop between AI search visibility and the pipeline and revenue outcomes leadership actually cares about.

How to Improve AI Search Visibility and Fix Inaccurate Answers

Once marketing tracks prompts and performance, it will reveal gaps, and once gaps are identified, marketing can construct a data-driven plan to close them.

The next section details some best practices to address common visibility and accuracy issues.

Strengthen entity consistency across the web.

AI platforms build their understanding of a brand from many sources at once, such as:

  • The company website.
  • Review sites.
  • Social profiles.
  • Directories.
  • Press mentions.

AI platforms pull information from across the web to create one synthesized answer. The best thing marketing can do is control the controllable, and, where possible, ensure that information is consistent and accurate.

For example, be consistent with the brand’s name, description, location, and core offering. Naturally, marketing can’t control everything, like a bad or incorrect review, but marketing combats negative sentiments with the truth. Plus, marketing can work with product teams or customer success to identify issues and prompt resolution.

Ultimately, AI platforms have a hard time confirming what’s correct if multiple versions of a narrative exist. That increases the odds of an inaccurate or inconsistent mention.

Build content that earns citations.

Page structure has been a topic in the world of search for many years. We all know that structuring pages well, with titles, headings, and body text, is good, but it’s possible to take things a step further for AI search.

For example, marketing can get super-specific about audiences and problems, creating pages around the exact problems buyers are having.

Answering questions directly, providing solutions, and backing them with claims with concrete details and data all make a page easier for AI platforms to lift from and cite.

For more information about writing for AI engines, read: How to Write Content that Generative AI Search Engines Will Cite, According to Experts

Correct inaccurate AI answers.

Inaccurate AI answers should trigger content updates, correction requests, and follow-up monitoring, especially if the inaccuracy is on owned media, like the brand’s website or Google Business Profile.

Tip: If you’re not sure where a piece of information has come from, because AI hasn’t cited anything, try searching for the information in Google and see what ranks. Look at your own website for inaccuracies. Let’s say an AI platform has cited your brand’s package as costing $69, but this price is over two years old, search in Google “site:yourwebsite.com $69.” This search would look for mentions of “$69” on your website. It’s possible the price is listed somewhere, like an old blog.

Expand presence across multiple channels.

AI platforms draw on a wide mix of sources, so a brand’s visibility is rarely built from its website alone. Active participation in industry discussions, consistent responses to reviews and feedback, and a presence across the platforms where a brand’s category gets discussed all contribute to how AI models perceive and describe a brand. The broader and more consistent that footprint, the more material AI platforms have to draw an accurate, favorable picture from.

Monitor for recurring issues.

A single inaccurate answer might be a one-off. The same issue appearing across multiple prompts or platforms is a pattern worth escalating. When negative sentiment or a factual error keeps showing up, it is worth routing that finding beyond marketing — into product, customer success, or support — since the underlying cause is often something those teams are better positioned to fix.

Best Tools to Track Brand Visibility In AI Search

The four tools below cover the full range of what a marketing team needs, from foundational SEO work to dedicated AEO tracking.

Marketing Hub SEO Marketing Software

This article focuses a lot on AEO and AI visibility, but AEO is not separate from SEO. Regardless of how many people search in AI, traditional SEO is still critical, more popular than AI search tools, and impactful on the sources that are mentioned and cited in AI tools.

Therefore, SEO tools are still a must.

Marketing Hub’s SEO tools lay the groundwork on which AI visibility depends‌.

Source

HubSpot’s SEO tools include an audit that surfaces prioritized fixes for on-site issues like broken links, missing meta descriptions, and thin content, then groups related content into topic clusters designed to build topical authority around core subjects rather than isolated keywords. It also pulls keyword data directly from Google Search Console, so marketing teams can see which queries are already driving organic traffic and which ones represent gaps worth closing.

What I like: Having data in one place is efficient. HubSpot allows integrations with Google Search Console, so data can be managed and checked from one place. The SEO recommendations are easy to use, written in plain English, and even have impact scores (high, medium, and low). The system names the person responsible for the fix, meaning tasks that keep SEO flowing are easily delegated.

HubSpot AEO

Source

HubSpot AEO is undoubtedly the core tool for ongoing AI visibility tracking. It provides marketers with four key capabilities:

  • A brand visibility score that tracks how often a brand appears across a set of tracked prompts.
  • Prompt-level tracking that shows the exact response each engine gave for each question.
  • Citation analysis that breaks down which domains and content types are earning references.
  • Competitor share of voice that shows how a brand’s mention rate stacks up against named competitors on the same prompts.

HubSpot AEO suggests a starting prompt set based on a brand’s industry, competitors, and business context, which can then be edited or expanded by the marketing humans in the team. Everything is trackable across major AI platforms like ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity, and results roll up into a dashboard that tracks visibility over time rather than showing a single static score.

Finally, recommendations turn the data into specific next actions:

  • Create a new page or update an existing one
  • Publish a LinkedIn post
  • Reach out to a third-party site for a mention.

One limitation worth flagging: Claude and Copilot are not currently tracked. For brands where either platform sends a meaningful share of AI referral traffic, that’s a real coverage gap to weigh before committing.

What I like: The recommendations and AI visibility tracking within HubSpot are absolutely useful and critical to marketing, but the real differentiator, in my opinion, is the CRM. Most AEO tools operate as a standalone dashboard, disconnected from what actually happens after a brand shows up in an AI answer.

HubSpot AEO doesn’t have that problem because it’s built on top of HubSpot CRM. The connection between marketing performance and sales matters more than ever. A visibility score sitting in isolation is just a vanity metric. What pays bills is knowing whether a mention, a citation, or a jump in share of voice actually turned into a contact, a deal, or revenue.

HubSpot AI Search Grader (free)

AI Search Grader is the place to start if marketing is new to AI brand visibility or tracking AI in any form.

AI Search Grader runs a one-time scored assessment of how ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity currently characterize a brand, scoring five dimensions out of a 100-point total:

  • Sentiment (40 points): The overall tone AI models use when describing a brand, evaluated across three layers: general tone, how that tone shifts across different topics and use cases, and the credibility of the sources shaping that characterization.
  • Presence Quality (20 points): How substantively AI platforms discuss the brand (“mention depth”), the quality of the sources feeding that understanding, and the overall richness of data available about the brand.
  • Brand Recognition (20 points): How widely the brand is recognized within AI training data itself.
  • Share of Voice (10 points): How often the brand is mentioned relative to competitors within the same set of responses.
  • Market Position (10 points): How the brand is positioned competitively compared to others in its category, based on how AI platforms describe its standing in the market.

The scoring is weighted toward sentiment because how a brand is described tends to matter more to buyers (and therefore marketing and sales) than simply whether it’s mentioned at all.

AI Search Grader runs against pre-set queries automatically, without requiring the marketer to write any prompts. ChatGPT and Gemini responses draw on model training data, while Perplexity’s results come from live web search, since Perplexity works differently under the hood. The tool also benchmarks a brand’s score against competitors, so the output reads more like a competitive snapshot than an isolated report card.

The trade-off is exactly what its name suggests: it’s a grader, not a tracker.

AI Search Grader captures one moment and doesn’t retain history or show trend lines, so running it repeatedly over time won’t build the kind of longitudinal data a brand needs to prove whether a strategy is working.

What I like: I always start with AI Search Grader for a benchmark, and I use it in pitches to show a brand exactly where it stands before any investment is made. It’s also my go-to when I want a read on competitors, but I can’t justify paying to track brand mentions in AI, like a secondary competitor that I’m curious about but don’t need tracked with full accuracy over time.

HubSpot AI Search Sensor

Source

HubSpot AI Search Sensor takes a different angle from the other three tools on this list.

It doesn’t track a specific brand at all.

It’s a free public dashboard built from anonymized HubSpot customer data, tracking industry-wide shifts in AI search behavior through three views:

  • AI-Referred Traffic Trends shows aggregate weekly traffic from ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity, useful for checking whether a brand’s own traffic dip reflects something brand-specific or a broader industry pattern.
  • AI Visibility Benchmarks by Industry shows visibility and citation share for a handful of representative brands across ten industries, giving a sense of what a “good” score looks like in a given category.
  • Citation Share Trends breaks down which content types (blog posts, product pages, listicles, and more) and which source channels (owned, earned, review sites, affiliate, and more) are earning citations, and how that mix is shifting week over week.

There’s also a daily Answer Engine Volatility Tracker, scoring how much answer engine behavior is shifting on a given day, from Calm through Extreme.

What I like: Marketing teams can use this broad data alongside their own AEO data: if a brand’s visibility score drops on a day when the volatility tracker also spikes, that points to a model update or algorithm shift rather than a brand-specific problem.

How to Connect AI Visibility to Content And Pipeline

AI visibility data should shape the content calendar directly. A low mention rate on a category prompt signals a content gap worth filling. A low citation rate on an existing page suggests the page needs restructuring, not replacing. A competitor winning share of voice on a comparison prompt means there’s a comparison page worth building.

This shifts content strategy from “what ranks” to “what gets cited and recommended.” The two overlap but aren’t identical — a page can rank well in Google and still get ignored by an AI platform if it doesn’t answer the question directly enough to lift and cite.

Connecting that data to pipeline is what makes the work defensible.

When visibility metrics sit in HubSpot’s CRM and marketing tools rather than a standalone dashboard, a content brief generated from a visibility gap can be tracked through to the campaign it supported and the deals that followed. That’s the difference between reporting a visibility score and reporting what the score was worth.

Frequently Asked Questions About Tracking AI Search Visibility

Which AI platforms should I prioritize first?

The AI platforms that any brand should prioritize should be decided based on data. Pull AI referral traffic from internal analytics. It will show which platform is dominating over the others and sending the most traffic. That platform is the one worth prioritizing first. However, from experience, the platforms to prioritize will probably be ChatGPT, Perplexity, Claude, or Copilot, plus AI Overviews within Google Search.

What’s the best way to organize prompts for consistent tracking?

Prompts hold up best when organized into a taxonomy covering brand, competitor, category, task-based, and comparison types, with the exact wording documented and reused every time a check runs.

How do I correct outdated or wrong information about my company in AI answers?

If an AI platform is describing a brand based on outdated pricing, an old feature list, or an incorrect description, the fix usually starts with the brand’s own website or Google Business Profile, since that’s the material marketing teams have the most control over.

How can I attribute AI search visibility to revenue?

Attribution starts with routing visibility data into the same system as customer and campaign data, rather than leaving it in a standalone dashboard. When AI visibility properties, prompt clusters, and citation data sit inside a CRM, marketing teams can connect a visibility gap to the content brief it produced, and that content to the campaign, contact, or deal that followed.

How often should we review and refresh our prompt library?

The prompt library itself needs a slower refresh cycle, revisited quarterly or whenever a brand launches a new product, enters a new category, or notices its keyword research and customer language shifting. Prompts that no longer reflect how buyers actually ask questions stop producing useful data, even if the tracking cadence around them stays consistent.

Tracking AI visibility isn’t optional anymore — search changed.

Failing to track AI visibility in 2026 and beyond is a failure to keep up with search, serve clients, and keep your brand at the top of prospective buyers’ minds.

For anyone starting from zero, HubSpot’s free AI Search Grader remains the fastest way to get a baseline read on where a brand currently stands, and HubSpot AEO is the natural next step once that baseline is set and marketing are ready to track mentions, citations, and sentiment across ChatGPT, Gemini, and Perplexity, all while feeding directly into the same CRM already running a brand’s marketing and sales data.

In my own client work, I’ve been tracking AI visibility for a year or two, and things are trending up for every single client, even those in niche B2B. For me, the major benefit of starting now is that brands have a benchmark and can see clearly how the search landscape is changing and how it’s impacting brand and visibility.

issues.title: Claude AI for marketing: How teams use it with HubSpot
