issues.title: 🔮 The $22 billion question about AI self-improvement #610
issues.summary: Plus: Cheap solar, who pays for Claude & DNA immunotherapy++
issues.author: Azeem Azhar
issues.content_html:
It’s simply the best, data-rich source for the money on how AI is reshaping the economy. — Matt G., a paying member

Subscribe now

My AI agent bought an iPhone for me this week. For an Uber, I’d still reach for the app.

That’s where we start today – I look at which jobs are worth handing over to AI, and why more Brits are paying for Claude. We’ll also look at what cheaper renewable power still needs and whether AI self-improvement owes more to intelligence or a massive research budget.

If you’re a member of Exponential View, join me in the subscriber chat:

Claude Britannia

Brits are spending more and more on AI. One in twenty adults in the UK pays for AI, spending more than $1.3 billion a year. Five percent is early days, but it is a fast ramp – it was 1% two years ago, and 2.5% a year ago. London is the hotspot; the professional skew is predictable, with those involved in tech, finance, education, and PR. And we are increasingly falling for Claude. Its share has quadrupled in a year.1 Was the trigger the improved harness on Claude Cowork?

Separately, made his first purchase using his Instinct agent, sweaters for winter. My Instinct agent secured my iPhone Duo for me on Tuesday. ’s agent booked a squash court for a showdown with . We’re playing around with them and finding them quite useful.

But in general, agent-based shopping is still early. Uber says four rides out of 320 million during Halloween week were booked by agents. I’m not sure I’d use an agent to book an Uber yet; hitting the app is easier. But getting an iPhone Duo, which involved checking Apple’s website every few minutes from 7 am, is a perfect job for them. So is finding finicky, complicated products like surge-protected power extensions, medicine pouches, or, in Will’s case, woolly jumpers.

Subscribe now

Fair-weather friends

The technology is doing its bit. Adding wind to solar and batteries cuts the median cost from $105 to $86 per MWh. North of Milan and Montreal (yes, they are on the same latitude), it falls from $164 to $99. Based on hourly modeling over ten years, and reckon that sun and wind mostly cover for each other – except for a difficult combined lull for about a week every four.

Ember also finds that 83% of the 750GW of fossil plants being planned sit where reliable renewables (with a bit of gas backup) cost under $100/MWh (which is roughly implied with oil at $60 a barrel).

My take is that technology costs will keep falling, and those that haven’t yet benefited from reductions (like panel installations) will start to yield as robotics improve. But redesigning the grid into a largely renewable-based one also requires more than better technology. It’ll need both a better cost of capital (gas plants still find capital cheaper than solar) and financial instruments that match energy prices to the volatility renewable-based energy brings.

issues.title: 🔮 What does it cost to make a worker?
issues.summary: Some early sketches of the economics of manufactured intelligence
issues.author: Azeem Azhar
issues.content_html:
Azeem’s sketchbook is an experimental format we’re trialing for paying members, where we share raw research notes, early frameworks, and unfinished ideas that haven’t been fully polished. They are the earliest indication of what I’m thinking through.

Here is another peek into my sketchbook. I’m trying to understand the economic trade-off between getting work done by an AI or a human. One way of doing this is to look at tasks in the economy and see how much it costs a human to do them compared to a machine.

Another way is to view the worker as an entity the economy needs, and to consider the minimum cost of creating one. (Of course, humans are much more than that, but I’m limiting the frame purely to economics here.) Those costs include the parenting, educating, and feeding from bairn to adult. We can then compare that to the cost of bringing in a machine capable of doing the same types of work using AI.

AI is manufactured intelligence. That is not the same intelligence that we humans have, but it’s clearly something that looks like intelligence.

While it is being manufactured, it’s highly replicable and follows the classic learning curve I described in my first book. And in my forthcoming second book, I extend these ideas.

Economically useful human intelligence is created very differently. It takes much longer than making a chip, and you don’t know the outcome for a long time.

issues.title: 🔥 Jensen Huang and the future of the AI boom
issues.summary: Good news for some, not so good news for others
issues.author: Azeem Azhar
issues.content_html:
Jensen Huang has resigned.

The company is in an awkward position, having refused to put a succession policy in place. Colette Kress, the CFO, will step in until it finds a replacement.

Company scandal aside, and there has been a lot, it’ll have a big impact on the AI boom.

Nvidia has been, without doubt, the linchpin of that boom. In the five years to 2026, the firm sold nearly 14 million flagship AI chips. They account for 85% of the market. The company has provided financial guarantees to the constellation of upstart AI infrastructure companies, the so-called neoclouds, so they can get their business moving. It has been a substantial venture capital backer of AI companies, with nearly $10 billion across Europe in the last year – the biggest investor there.

The numbers don’t do justice to how important Jensen himself has been. This isn’t like Apple without Steve Jobs. When Steve Jobs relinquished the CEO role in 2011, shortly before he passed away, he left a well-briefed successor and a management team known to customers and the market alike. And if Nvidia has been the linchpin of the AI boom, Jensen has been the linchpin of Nvidia.

I thought of him as the person with the best visibility into what was going on in AI, simply because everything ran on his chips. He advocated open-source models, including, uncomfortably now, Chinese ones. And pushed for a more accommodating approach to China.

I’ve seen him in London a couple of times. Once, he arrived on stage from down the street with then-Prime Minister Keir Starmer in tow. He brings energy and hands out billions of dollars. Calling out a startup’s name, followed by “I’m backing you with $500m” or whatever the number was. He returned a printout of our State of the AI Economy report, his signature across the front in gold marker, telling me it would be worth more now. Maybe even more after today.

The linchpin seems to be made less of solid steel and more of a well-worn leather. Will the ecosystem that depends on it stay on the road?

The current wave of AI investments, in model makers and infrastructure, is predicated on massive customer demand, not rampant oversupply. The industry’s common refrain over the past two years has been consistent: we are short on capacity. Not tomorrow, but today. That is why the spot prices for AI chips stay high even as they age. It’s why Anthropic has lined up $900bn of computing supply over the next 15 to 20 years – to make sure they don’t run short.

We’ve estimated that in the last 12 months, total revenues in the AI sector (outside of China) came to $188bn, growing faster than 4.2x a year. About 75% of that ends up at the infrastructure layer: the companies that own and operate the chips that do the calculations that make ChatGPT run for you.

The vast majority of revenue comes from chips made by Nvidia.

And the lack of capacity is what has created opportunities for new infrastructure companies, the so-called neoclouds. These young pups don’t have the track record of Microsoft or Google, so they have had to lean on Nvidia, their main supplier, for various kinds of guarantees. These guarantees range from the reasonably above-board to things that smell circular. While the numbers are large, for some companies (like Anthropic or XAI), Nvidia’s contribution is not a do-or-die proportion. But the man behind it all is leaving the building.

Demand stays

issues.title: Voyager 1 at one light-day: Historian revisits Golden Record's forgotten details
issues.summary: "They are pretty confident that it's going to last a long, long, long time..."
issues.author: Robert Pearlman
issues.content_html:
In the one light-day that humanity's most distant object has now traveled from Earth, there has been enough time for details about its creation—and what it left behind—to be discovered again.

Voyager 1, which left Earth in 1977 on an initial mission to fly by Jupiter and Saturn (as well as the latter's moon Titan), crossed into interstellar space in 2012. Like its twin (Voyager 2), Voyager 1 carries a "commemorative phonograph record," in part as a nod to the 100th anniversary of the recording medium and as a message from humanity to whomever (or whatever) encounters the spacecraft on its journey through outer space.

About those forgotten bits, ask Glen Swanson. While researching the history of the Golden Record, he uncovered the discs' overlooked second set of operating directions and located the duplicates that were made and distributed almost five decades ago.

issues.title: Grand Theft Auto VI: The Ars Technica review
issues.summary: Jason and Lucia's crime-heavy love story fuels a wonder of digital urban simulation.
issues.author: Kyle Orland
issues.content_html:
Just a minute ago, I was shooting my way out of a cocaine deal gone wrong, darting behind furniture for cover. Now I’m sitting on the floor of my home, working through the instructions to construct an Ikea-style coffee table with my partner. A tiny heart with a plus sign pops up, showing that our relationship is stronger for this quotidian domestic effort.

This is the contrast at the heart of Grand Theft Auto VI, a game that seems to revel in both action movie bombast and the mundanities of everyday life for an up-and-coming young criminal couple.

The reimagined and expanded Vice City is still the grand, crude, satirical criminal playground you’d expect after 25 years of 3D Grand Theft Auto games. And that world is as full, detailed, technically impressive, and polished as you would expect after this latest installment received a reported billion-dollar budget and roughly a decade of development work involving thousands of Rockstar staffers.

issues.summary: Word, Excel, and PowerPoint now live inside Copilot; always-on agents are next.
issues.author: Nick Indge
issues.content_html:
Opening the keynote at its Ignite event, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella outlined the company's vision for its new "frontier ecosystem," announcing Tuesday the general availability of Word, Excel, and PowerPoint inside Copilot, which he described as "the new OS for work."

The announcement is a striking inversion of how we've traditionally used software. Rather than an app like Word being the attraction and Clippy the assistant to help you use it, Microsoft envisions the new Copilot integrations will see agents driving things, with the software packages riding shotgun. Applications will become plugin components of the agent's work, backed by an organizational knowledge layer that draws context from emails, meetings, calendars, chats, and files. Users will now be able to create documents, spreadsheets, and presentations directly in Copilot, with the resulting files remaining editable in their respective Office applications.

issues.title: We built the AI study tool every parent wants. Almost nobody used it
issues.summary: Motivation comes from people.
issues.author: Roee Naim
issues.content_html:
I run Tutorela, a U.S. tutoring marketplace that sells human tutoring, with AI for students between sessions. I’m saying that up front because this piece argues for that model, and because we learned the lesson behind it the hard way.

Alpha School has become the national test case for AI-first education, and it’s now expanding into public schools in Texas and South Carolina. As districts decide how much of the school day to hand to software, they should hear what happened when we gave students the best learning tool we could build.

We built it. They didn’t come.

For 15 years we’ve run Limud Naim, a tutoring marketplace in Israel whose tutors have taught more than 500,000 private lessons. To fill the gap between those lessons, we built a math learning and practice app with more than 10,000 exercises. Every problem came with a full solution in text and video, and we made the whole thing a game, with progress and rewards, so practice would feel less like homework. A year ago we added an AI assistant that could walk a student through any step, any time, for free.

By any product standard it was the best a student could get. Only about 10% of students used it, and most of those who started didn’t stick around. The exercises were excellent and the AI was patient and clear, but none of that mattered, because the students weren’t showing up.

We’re not the only ones.

A two-year randomized trial in 18 Tennessee middle schools, published this year by the National Bureau of Economic Research, found the same thing with Khanmigo, Khan Academy’s AI tutor. Nearly every student tried it, but the median student messaged it on only a third of the days they practiced, and in only 17% of the practice sessions where they made a mistake. Most messages were one- or two-word answers or clicks on suggested prompts. The math gains matched what Khan Academy practice delivers without any AI. Khan Academy itself says only about 15% of students with access to Khanmigo engage with it. “It may be that human attention is the key ingredient,” the researchers wrote.

Then we added one person.

At Limud Naim we didn’t change the app. We changed who was in charge of it. Each student’s tutor began managing their learning: picking the practice that fit where the student was, assigning it, and following up at the next lesson.

Everything changed. More than half of the students who got assignments from their tutor completed them, up from about 10% who used the app on their own. It was the same app with the same exercises. The only new ingredient was a human who knew the student and expected the work to get done.

That result is why we built Tutorela as a hybrid from day one.

Motivation comes from people.

This is the part AI-first education gets wrong. The bet behind an AI-run school day is that if content is personalized enough and feedback is instant enough, students will learn. Our experience and the Khanmigo data both say content was never the bottleneck. Students already have more free, high-quality explanations than any generation in history. What they’re missing is someone who notices whether they did the work and cares how it went.

A child practices fractions on a Tuesday night because their tutor, whom they’ll see on Thursday, asked them to. AI can generate the perfect worksheet, but it can’t make a 12-year-old feel that someone is counting on them.

Where AI actually belongs

None of this makes me an AI skeptic. I believe AI makes tutoring better, as long as the tutor sets the direction. Then AI makes the time between lessons count: it answers the question at 9 p.m., explains a step a third time without frustration, and offers more practice than any human could grade. The tutor gets a better-prepared student, and the student gets help exactly when they’re stuck.

Put AI in charge and remove the human, and the system loses its engine. You keep the explanations and lose the reason to show up.

What schools and parents should take from this

For school leaders weighing AI-heavy models, the question isn’t whether the software is good. It usually is, and ours was too. The question is who will hold each student accountable for using it. If the answer is “the software,” expect what we and the Tennessee researchers saw: wide access, thin engagement, and students who quietly stop.

For parents, the advice is simple. Use AI tools, but pair them with a person, whether a tutor, a teacher, or a parent who checks in, who sets the goals and follows up.

The future of learning isn’t AI instead of teachers. It’s a teacher in charge, with AI for everything in between.

The real test is not whether a company can succeed in a market once. It is whether it can keep adapting as consumers and technology evolve. It is no longer enough for leaders to see where the future is headed. The best leaders build organizations capable of riding on the opportunities and challenges.

issues.title: Nvidia posts a blockbuster quarter as Jensen Huang’s dealmaking legacy hangs in the balance
issues.summary: Colette Kress says Nvidia will be “disciplined" with its money. She stopped short of saying whether the company would match Huang’s pace of AI investment.
issues.author: Morgan Chittum
issues.content_html:
Morgan Chittum here. Nvidia posted quarterly results late Tuesday that handily beat earnings and revenue expectations—just days after Jensen Huang resigned as CEO following reports of extramarital affairs. The upheaval sent the stock to its lowest level in well over a year. The better-than-expected fiscal third quarter may give public-market investors a reprieve. But a massive question still hangs over the AI-pilled private markets, where Nvidia poured billions into investments and financing under Huang’s leadership: Will Colette Kress, the longtime CFO now serving as interim CEO, match his appetite for bankrolling the AI boom?

Before we get to that, the numbers deserve their due: Nvidia had a very good quarter. Revenue for the three months ended October 25 came in at $115.8 billion, more than double the $57 billion recorded a year earlier and above analysts’ expectations of around $109 billion. Adjusted earnings per share were $2.68, topping estimates of $2.48. The company forecasted fourth-quarter revenue of $130 billion, plus or minus 3%—a range that clears analysts’ $125 billion estimate even at the low end. Management also raised its growth forecast for the fiscal year ending in January 2028 to 75%, from 70%.

Stratospheric revenue growth, insatiable demand for chips. It’s almost business as usual for the world’s leading AI chipmaker. “Our momentum is real. Our demand is accelerating. Our supply is growing. Our customers and our partners are with us, and employees are committed. We’ve got this,” Kress said.

There’s more to the Nvidia story than blowout earnings, though. Over 33 years as CEO, Huang turned Nvidia into what some have characterized as the “central bank of AI.” It gets at the idea that Allie explored last week: Huang is AI’s ultimate key man. Under his leadership, Nvidia’s share of the global market for AI and data center GPUs swelled to north of 80%. The company also invested in 126 startups this year alone, including heavyweights like Anthropic and OpenAI. Not to mention its announced $13 billion acquisition of leading open-source repository Hugging Face.

And that’s before you get to all the financing Huang has championed. In August, Nvidia announced a memorandum of understanding—essentially a preliminary agreement—with some of Wall Street’s biggest firms: Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield Asset Management, Goldman Sachs and KKR. The goal is to raise more than $500 billion in third-party capital for AI infrastructure. Those talks are still underway, Reutersreported Monday, with no indication from Nvidia of a pause. But with its chief dealmaker gone, will Kress keep the money moving?

Although earnings didn’t give us an explicit answer, Kress hinted at a more measured approach than Huang’s. The ex-CFO, who held the job for more than 13 years, said she was proud of Nvidia’s role in supporting the broader AI ecosystem. But she also said the company would “remain thoughtful” and “disciplined” in committing capital, adding that Nvidia is “rigorously evaluating” future guarantees, investments and commitments. Last week, TheWall Street Journalreported, citing people familiar with the matter, that Kress had questioned some of Nvidia’s dealmaking under Huang.

One thing Kress won’t have to worry about, however, is Huang returning to the top job.

Hours before Nvidia reported Tuesday, Huang said he’d love to have his old job back if the board asked. Board chair Harvey Jones said on the earnings call that there were no plans to reinstate him. So Huang won’t be taking the helm anytime soon—at Nvidia, at least.

See you tomorrow,

Morgan Chittum

issues.title: Does the Nvidia turmoil spell trouble for the Gulf’s AI ambitions?
issues.summary: From Abu Dhabi’s mega AI campus to Saudi Arabia’s data center ambitions, the Gulf has placed a huge bet on Nvidia. Now, turmoil at the heart of the chipmaker threatens to complicate the region’s high-stakes AI ambitions.
issues.author: Melissa Hancock
issues.content_html:
The downfall of Jensen Huang following revelations of extramarital affairs—including one involving a suspected Chinese spy—and the turmoil that has engulfed Nvidia in its wake have gripped the world’s attention over the past week.

Given their national AI ambitions are strongly tied to investments in Nvidia and access to its coveted chips, Gulf countries will be vulnerable to any dramatic changes in its future strategy.

During U.S. President Donald Trump’s Gulf tour in May 2025, the UAE unveiled plans to develop a 5-GW joint AI Campus in Abu Dhabi. Once complete, it will be the largest facility of its kind outside the U.S. At the heart of the project is Stargate UAE, a 1-GW computing cluster developed by Abu Dhabi-backed G42 in partnership with a host of U.S. companies, including Nvidia, which will supply its Grace Blackwell chips (GB300s).

Nvidia has also forged a strong commercial alliance with Saudi Arabia, with Huang among a select group of U.S. tech leaders invited to meet with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman during his much-feted visit to the White House last November.

During the visit, Elon Musk announced a 500-MW data center in partnership with Saudi government-backed AI company, Humain, which will be powered by Nvidia’s computing chips.

Trump also hosted Mohammed bin Salman, alongside Huang and Elon Musk, at the U.S.-Saudi Investment Forum on November 19 last year.

Just hours later, the U.S. Commerce Department authorized the export of up to 35,000 Nvidia Blackwell GB300 chips to both G42 and Humain. Earlier in the day, Humain said it planned to purchase 600,000 Nvidia AI chips.

This relationship was deepened last month when Humain announced plans with Nvidia to deploy around 27,000 GPUs and develop up to 84-MW of AI computing capacity in the kingdom across a multi-phase program starting in the fourth quarter of this year and followed by planned large-scale deployments beginning in mid-2027.

While the existing partnerships Nvidia holds with the UAE and Saudi are unlikely to be threatened by Huang’s departure, it could weaken the relationship’s momentum, according to Mohammed Soliman, senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, where he focuses on technology and geopolitics.

“The relationship with Nvidia is pretty solid and institutional at this point,” he said. “The deals with G42 and Humain sit on government-to-government agreements that were already in place. That said, Jensen matters a lot and his leaving will have an impact. The overall direction doesn’t change, but losing him as the main driver takes something off the table.”

Sam Winter-Levy, a senior fellow in the Technology and International Affairs program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, expects that the change in leadership at Nvidia could make the company more circumspect in its business dealings with the Gulf.

“Huang was the public face of Nvidia’s sovereign AI pitch and had his own relationships with Gulf leaders, which will be hard to replace quickly,” said Winter-Levy, whose research focuses on the geopolitics of AI.

“I would assume Nvidia will honor its existing contracts with the Gulf, probably with more attention to compliance and things like end-use checks, but to make fewer splashy announcements of new deals.”

In July, Washington relaxed export restrictions on the UAE, granting approved organizations greater access to Nvidia chips and other advanced technologies.

For Gulf governments, a more immediate concern is whether the upheaval at Nvidia could make Washington more reluctant to approve further exports of advanced chips, thereby slowing the pace of the region’s AI buildout.

The upheaval has given U.S. lawmakers fresh ammunition to push for the inclusion of a series of chip-control bills, such as the AI Overwatch Act, the Chip Security Act and the MATCH Act, in this year’s National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA).

Last week, Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer urged Congress to pass the bills, while House Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar called for chip export controls to be included in the annual defense policy bill.

“Congress has limited direct power here, since export licenses lie with the executive branch, and the administration has removed many of the license requirements that slowed chip deliveries to the UAE in the past,” said Winter-Levy.

“But oversight raises the political cost of new Gulf deals, and Congress can attach conditions such as chip location verification to new bills like the NDAA.”

Chip location verification is a technical and regulatory method used to track the physical location of advanced processors—such as GPUs—to ensure they do not get smuggled or diverted to restricted countries.

However, on Monday, the U.S. Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security issued an interim rule that requires licences for global transfers of AI chips and servers to data centers worldwide.if the equipment could be used by 22 embargoed countries which includes China. The move aims to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies to lease Nvidia’s computing power from locations in other countries.

“The new remote access rule primarily affects Gulf companies if they are renting large amounts of compute to Chinese-parented firms, but otherwise does not fundamentally change the situation for the UAE,” said Winter-Levy.

“It does, however, signal that the administration is increasingly prepared to crack down on chip diversion and remote access if it becomes politically salient enough.”

Looking ahead, it seems increasingly likely that the Gulf will become more vulnerable to U.S. export controls given that, even before Huang’s abrupt departure, Democratic lawmakers had already pushed back against what they viewed as its preferential treatment. They frequently cited fears that China could access sensitive U.S. technology through the Gulf.

“There will probably be more political noise out of Washington that could slow some deliveries or stretch timelines,” said Soliman.

However, the region’s growing role in financing and supporting America’s AI infrastructure could also give the region some leverage in return, according to Winter-Levy.

“The dependence isn’t entirely one-way,” he said. “Gulf capital is now part of the American AI buildout, which gives them some leverage. And if U.S. companies come to rely on large quantities of compute housed in the Gulf, that will give the Gulf a degree of leverage over those companies. But the asymmetry is large, since Washington can slow the Gulf’s AI plans with a regulatory notice.”

Ultimately, Nvidia’s upheaval is unlikely to derail the Gulf’s AI ambitions, but it exposes just how dependent those ambitions remain on decisions made in Washington and Silicon Valley.

The UAE and Saudi Arabia have invested heavily in positioning themselves as global AI powerhouses, but their ability to deliver on those plans hinges on continued access to U.S. technology and political goodwill.

As scrutiny of chip exports intensifies, the challenge for both countries will be to maintain their strategic partnerships while reducing their exposure to shifting U.S. political priorities. For the Gulf, the question is no longer simply whether Nvidia can deliver the chips, but whether Washington will continue to let them.

issues.title: U.S. export controls and Nvidia’s leadership transition remain key watchpoints for the Gulf
issues.summary: In this week’s Fortune Gulf Brief.
issues.author: Melissa Hancock
issues.content_html:
Welcome to this week’s Fortune Gulf Brief. We’ll be covering:

  • Nvidia’s strong results offer relief, but Gulf’s AI ambitions remain exposed
  • Masdar doubles down on U.S. renewables
  • Gulf oil surge pushes global market back into surplus
  • And, the three we enjoyed reading this week

Nvidia’s solid third-quarter results will no doubt reassure Gulf investors that the U.S. chipmaking giant is on course to maintain a healthy growth trajectory despite the resignation of Jensen Huang.

Nvidia reported revenue of $116 billion for the three months to October, up 103% from a year ago, and above Wall Street estimates of $109 billion. It has beaten estimates in each of the last five quarters.

For the Gulf states, which are betting big on AI to help move their economies away from oil and rely on Nvidia’s advanced chips to achieve that, the company’s future success is critical.

Huang’s affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy has heightened political pressure to tighten export controls amid long-running concerns in the U.S. that China’s access to advanced American AI chips could undermine national security.

It is also likely to sharpen scrutiny of Nvidia’s future dealings with the Gulf as part of a broader effort to prevent China from accessing banned American technology via intermediaries.

Such concerns have previously made securing Nvidia’s advanced chips an uphill battle for regional AI champions such as PIF-owned HUMAIN and Abu Dhabi-backed G42.

In July, the U.S. Department of Commerce loosened export restrictions on the UAE so that approved government agencies and entities—including its tech champion G42—can receive advanced computing hardware, including from Nvidia, under broader license exceptions. The rule change set no caps on how many chips or other sophisticated goods can be sold to those entities.

Democratic China hawks have frequently raised the alarm over the large-scale sales of AI chips to the Gulf region, arguing they could give China backdoor access to U.S. technology. Last May, Democratic senators demanded that AI chip deals with Saudi Arabia and the UAE contain adequate guardrails to prevent the leakage of sensitive technology to China.

Both Gulf countries maintain strong commercial ties to Chinese tech entities.

In September, Chinese tech giant Alibaba Cloud announced plans to ramp up its data center capacity and expand localized AI services across the UAE. Meanwhile, in Riyadh, Lenovo unveiled its first laptop made in Saudi Arabia at its sprawling 200,000-square-meter manufacturing facility, developed as part of a $2 billion partnership with Alat, a subsidiary of Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF).

In its first policy response to the Nvidia scandal, on Monday the U.S. Commerce Department introduced an interim rule requiring overseas data centers to obtain a government license before supplying “significant volumes of computing power” to firms with headquarters in 22 embargoed countries, including China. The move aims to close a loophole that has allowed Chinese companies to lease Nvidia’s computing power from locations in other countries.

With Democrats holding majorities in both chambers of Congress from January next year, increased congressional scrutiny of Gulf AI deals is likely.

More broadly, the Gulf’s exposure to the volatility in AI stock prices has been further rattled by Jensen’s resignation amid a broader sell-off in AI tech stocks over the past few months, on the back of valuation and investment bubble concerns.

While not all Gulf funds disclose their individual investments, publicly available filings suggest that Gulf sovereign wealth funds, such as Mubadala, have relatively limited direct exposure to Nvidia shares compared to the scale of their investments in other tech firms.

According to the consultancy, Global SWF, Mubadala ranks among the top institutional backers of AI worldwide.

MGX, an AI and advanced tech investment firm backed by Mubadala, holds stakes and has participated in funding rounds for OpenAI, Anthropic, xAI, Databricks, GlobalFoundries,Isomorphic Labs, andSpaceX.

Saudi’s PIF-backed AI venture HUMAIN invested $3 billion in xAI’s $20 billion Series E round in February, shortly before it merged with SpaceX.

Global SWF estimates that Mubadala’s portfolio may have declined by $17.5 billion since the onset of the AI selloff at the end of June, largely driven by a more than 50% drop in chipmaker GlobalFoundries’ share price. PIF, meanwhile, is estimated to have suffered a $5.6 billion decline in the value of its AI-related holdings, largely attributable to its stake in SpaceX.

“Indirectly and strategically, Gulf wealth funds are exposed to the current market turbulence,” Sam Winter-Levy, a senior fellow in the Technology and International Affairs program at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, told me.

“MGX and other Gulf vehicles hold large stakes in AI labs, data center platforms, and other companies whose valuations depend on the AI boom—and Nvidia, of course, is central to that boom. The Gulf’s national AI strategies are built on Nvidia hardware. I think a prolonged loss of confidence in Nvidia would hit the Gulf relatively hard.”

In a research note published on Monday, London-headquartered Capital Economics warned that the ongoing shakeout in the AI sector is setting the stage for a larger downturn in the U.S. equity market over the next year.

With Nvidia considered a bellwether for the AI industry, its results should help to calm the markets and buoy investor sentiment ahead of Anthropic’s planned listing on Thursday.

Backed by MGX and the Qatar Investment Authority, the Claude developer’s listing is expected to value the business at $1.4 trillion. It has been reported that the shares could be six times oversubscribed.

You can read my piece here, which takes a closer look at what the potential fallout from the Nvidia crisis could mean for the Gulf’s AI ambitions, particularly in terms of its planned data center buildout.

Melissa Hancock

And as ever, thanks for reading, and do keep in touch with your thoughts and ideas.

issues.content_html:
More than a decade after Grand Theft Auto V was first released, its sequel is finally launching. On November 19th, GTA VI will be available on both the PS5 and Xbox Series X / S, and it’s quite possibly the most anticipated video game launch of all time.

Part of this has to do with the success of its predecessor, as GTA V sold more than 230 million copies over the last 13 years. Some of it has to do with the sheer length of time between releases, a period that was plagued by leaks and a handful of delays that made the wait even harder for fans.

But GTA VI is now a real thing you can play, and you can also keep track of all of the important post-launch information right here. That includes our own review and interviews with the development team, as well as news on just how the game ends up resonating with players.

issues.title: Is Dominica Worth Visiting? (Don’t make the mistakes I made!)
issues.summary: Is Dominica worth visiting? After six challenging days on the island, my honest answer is: only for a certain kind of traveler. My husband Charlie and I visited Dominica in December 2025, and it was the toughest stop by far on our four-week trip across the Caribbean. We dealt with some of the worst roads I’ve […] The post Is Dominica Worth Visiting? (Don’t make the mistakes I made!) appeared first
issues.author: Adventurous Kate
issues.content_html:
Is Dominica worth visiting? After six challenging days on the island, my honest answer is: only for a certain kind of traveler.

My husband Charlie and I visited Dominica in December 2025, and it was the toughest stop by far on our four-week trip across the Caribbean.

We dealt with some of the worst roads I’ve ever experienced, nearly constant rain, and a horrible last night spent searching for food near the airport.

Part of the problem was our expectations. Almost everything I’d read about Dominica in travel media, from “the nature island” tagline to the gorgeous waterfall roundups, made it sound like an unspoiled paradise, the ultimate gem, the place that would be everyone’s favorite island if only they knew it existed.

I knew not to expect great beaches. What I didn’t know was how much effort it would take just to get from one place to another, or how stressful those drives would be.

Planning your trip to Dominica soon?

Dominica’s tourism is growing every year, and many small guesthouses and tours fill up quickly. Book ahead to avoid disappointment!

Top Experiences and Tours in Dominica:

  1. VIP Tour: Trafalgar Falls, Sulfur Spa, and Beach (Includes my favorite hot spring!)
  2. Waterfalls, Titou Gorge, and Spa (Cool gorge swimming and my fave hot spring)
  3. Waitukubuli Volcano Snorkeling (Unique snorkel adventure)

Top-Rated Hotels in Dominica:

  1. Secret Bay (THE best small luxury hotel on the island)
  2. Kootney Resorts (I stayed here — nice midrange cottages in Portsmouth)
  3. Fort Young Hotel (Small hotel with infinity pool in Roseau)
  4. Ti Kwen Glo Cho (Spend one night at these hot springs!)

Best Dominica eSIM:I recommend an Holafly eSIM to stay connected in Dominica. Get 5% off with code HOLAKATE.

Renting a car in Dominica?Find deals on car rental rates here (but make sure you read about the reality of driving here first).

I’ve wondered for so long if I should even write this post. Not because I struggle to tell the truth — the number-one thing I hear from my readers is “You’re so honest!” — but because I don’t want to hurt a struggling island.

Dominica is still rebuilding after Hurricane Maria, and Dominicans are working hard to grow their tourism industry the right way. The last thing I want to do is punch down.

I’ve realized the most useful thing I can do is be honest but fair about the mistakes we made and what you should do differently on your trip, dear readers.

So grab yourself a cup of tea and sit back to read about one of the most lush and vibrant places I’ve ever visited: an island that is spectacularly beautiful, often deeply frustrating, and full of wonderful people who deserve a break.

This post was published in November 2026.

Is Dominica underrated, or unpopular for a reason?

Dominica occupies a unique position in travel media. Most people don’t know this island even exists, or they mix it up with the Dominican Republic.

It’s easy to see why. Dominica has no big, sandy beaches and very few large beach resorts, which keeps away mass-market tourism. Its small airport can’t handle large jets, so getting here usually means connecting through another island.

Most visitors arrive on cruise ships, spend a few hours on an excursion, and leave by dinnertime. Even some Caribbean aficionados haven’t heard of Dominica.

Dominicans are well aware of this. Thea Lafond-Gadson won Dominica’s first-ever Olympic medal, a gold, in the triple jump at the 2024 Summer Olympics in Paris, and I remember her press conference immediately after:

Okay, we’ll start with the basics. My country’s name is Dominica. We are not Dominican Republic, so it’s pronounced differently. We are about roughly 70,000 people, not 7 million, not 70 million, 70,000. And it is a gorgeous, gorgeous gem in the Caribbean.

And among the travel writers who DO know Dominica, the coverage is almost universally glowing.

Dominica is “the nature island.” Dominica is the greenest island. Dominica is the “most authentic” Caribbean island (if there were a measure for authenticity, but I digress…) Dominica is the island of 365 rivers. Dominica is the Caribbean the way it used to be.

What you rarely read is what it’s actually like to get around, where to find food, or how much it rains. And it was in this context that I planned our trip.

Dominica has been through a lot.

The most important thing to know before visiting is that Dominica has gone through some very difficult times.

In 2015, Tropical Storm Erika caused deadly flooding and landslides. Two years later, Hurricane Maria destroyed homes and infrastructure across the island, with damage and losses estimated at 1.37 billion USD. Thirty people were confirmed dead; a similar number were reported missing.

The damage was more than twice the size of Dominica’s GDP. Imagine a single storm wiping out more than two years of everything your country produces.

Dominica is still rebuilding today, and a lot of what frustrated me as a visitor, especially the roads, traces back to the damage of those storms. It’s important to keep this context in mind as you read this post.

Our Itinerary

After doing some research, we decided we would fly in and out of Dominica, rent a car for the duration of our trip, and spend six nights based in Portsmouth, Dominica’s second city, in the northwest.

For accommodation, we booked Kootney Resorts, with cottage-style accommodation.

In terms of activities, this is what we chose to prioritize:

  • Taking a boat ride on the Indian River
  • Visiting Cabrits National Park
  • Exploring Morne Trois Pitons National Park, the island’s sole UNESCO World Heritage Site
  • Hiking to Middleham Falls
  • Soaking in the hot springs in Wotten Waven

There is one prominent activity in Dominica we chose not to do: the Boiling Lake Hike.

Dominica is home to one of only two boiling lakes in the world (the other is in New Zealand), and that’s normally the type of activity I’d be keen to experience.

But the hike is very challenging, with lots of vertical climbs, and takes around 6-8 hours, and Charlie and I didn’t want to commit to a hike that was both long and difficult.

Another special activity in Dominica is swimming with sperm whales, but these are done as weeklong trips, not a day activity.

Arrival in Dominica

We arrived at Douglas-Charles Airportin Dominica via direct flight from Barbados and picked up our rental SUV.

In Dominica, they drive on the left side of the road. As Charlie is a Brit and I haven’t driven on the left in anything bigger than a Thai motorbike, we decided he would do the driving.

Dominica’s airport is located in Marigot, in the less-developed northeast of the island. This is far from Roseau, Dominica’s capital, largest city, ferry hub, and cruise port, which is in the southwest.

We set out for our accommodation in the town of Portsmouth, on the northwest corner of the island.

And so began one of the most terrifying drives of my life.

The roads between the airport and Portsmouth were in horrible condition — narrow, full of potholes, lots of switchbacks, and with deep trenches dug on each side. Not ordinary trenches. These were so wide that if you drove onto them, your car would flip over, and much of the time they were obscured by unkempt vegetation.

And that’s not all. Our flight had been delayed a few hours, so the sun set in the middle of our drive. We drove through the darkness as trucks, often with no lights on, passed us while beeping.

Charlie is a skilled driver — I trust him. But this drive was so frightening, I could barely move, my heart thudding the whole time. Google Maps said the drive would take around an hour; it took closer to two.

Once we arrived at our cottage, I collapsed in relief, my hands still shaking. And all I could think about was, We’ll need to drive BACK to the airport, too.

Settling In, and a River Journey

The owner of our cottage at Kootney Resorts, Trish, had told us not to worry about checking in that night and to just get some sleep and come by in the morning. So we walked to a Chinese restaurant down the street for a quick dinner of lo mein and fried rice.

A Chinese place? Yes.

Once you start noticing Chinese construction in Dominica, you see it everywhere: signs on building sites, Chinese crews, Chinese restaurants, and the massive new Chinese-built international airport under construction on the northeast coast.

This isn’t an accident. It goes back to 2004, when Dominica cut diplomatic ties with Taiwan in favor of Beijing. This triggered a wave of Chinese grant-financed infrastructure projects in Dominica.

China initially committed $112 million USD to Dominica in 2004; the projects have only increased since then. China also helped fund rebuilding after Hurricane Maria in 2017, including six new schools.

But why is China spending all this money? The Chinese government wants more nations to side with China and no longer recognize Taiwan. Dominica is one of many Caribbean nations where China is doing this. As always, China is playing the long game.

(This is a very interesting story, and The People’s Map: Dominica has a great read on it.)

That next morning, we headed out for a riverboat trip with Indian River Tours at 8:00 AM. I had WhatsApped the company the night before, and our guide, Dexter, encouraged us to come for an early tour to enjoy the river before the cruise ship day-trippers showed up.

Together with a French couple, we glided down the peaceful Indian River, tall palm trees poking into the stormy sky. Dominica claims to have 365 rivers — though let’s just say they have a generous definition of “river” — and they give the landscape life.

Pirates of the Caribbean: Dead Man’s Chest was shot in part here, and we got to see a piece of the remaining set: Tia Dalma’s shack!

We arrived at our eventual destination, a bar set in the woods, where Dexter took us on a short walk. Charlie and I played with a little brown tabby cat we named Domingo (it was Sunday, after all!).

Our tour cost $25 USD each, or 68 East Caribbean Dollars (XCD). (Many places in Dominica quote prices in USD, but XCD is more widely accepted than USD and you will almost certainly get change in XCD.)

Dexter told us we had to buy a national park pass, and we got one at a nearby gas station. National park passes are either $5 USD for one site or $12 USD for one week.

After the river trip, we went for breakfast at a cafe called Water’s Edge, a lovely little spot in Portsmouth with hearty Dominican dishes and drool-worthy baked goods. Praise music blared on the radio as we devoured an enormous pair of cookies.

Next, we hit up a local grocery store for provisions, buying a little can of jerk Vienna sausages out of curiosity. A woman walked down the aisles, her phone on speakerphone, blasting a sermon.

If you somehow ended up in Dominica on a Sunday and had no idea which day of the week it was, I think you’d figure it out pretty quickly.

Back at Kootney Resorts, we checked in with the owner, Trish. A longtime expat living in Dominica, Trish welcomed us with big hugs, gave us travel tips, and encouraged us to swim or even bathe in the creek behind her house.

Overall, we liked our cottage — it had decent internet, good cooking equipment, the AC worked well, and the covered porch was nice, even when it rained. Restaurants and the grocery store were a quick drive or a 10-minute walk away.

I highly recommend this place if you want to stay in Portsmouth, and Trish is a lovely person.

That afternoon, we made the short drive to Cabrits National Park. Located on the edge of Portsmouth, it’s the smallest of the three national parks on the island. Here we explored Fort Shirley, a British garrison edged with cannons.

That day, a Ritz-Carlton Yacht Collection ship was docked just off the park. (While most cruise ships dock in Roseau, some smaller ships dock here in Portsmouth.) And I won’t lie — it looked like a VERY NICE place to spend a vacation!

Cabrits National Park is also home to some short and easy hiking trails. We walked down a few of them.

To be honest, Cabrits National Park is nothing special — I don’t think it’s necessary to visit, and it’s definitely not worth paying for an additional national park pass unless you already have a weekly pass.

After the park, we drove up the coastline to the towns of Savanne Paille and Toucari, and once again I held my breath as Charlie drove those twisted, hilly, rugged roads.

But the journey was worth it. While the conventional wisdom is that Dominica is not a place you come to for beaches, there were actually a few nice ones up here.

The beaches themselves were narrow, with not much room to spread out, but they were pretty, with calm water and gorgeous sunset views.

We grabbed some sodas at a beach bar called Keepin It Real and enjoyed shrimp and macaroni pie at Roots Rock Bar & Grill. The sunset that night was purple and lovely.

Also on this part of the island? The InterContinental Resort, with a long driveway leading up to the luxurious grounds. Charlie and I wondered if they offered day passes.

Oh, and they did. But something else came up first.

So Much Rain

By the time we arrived in Dominica, Charlie and I had been in the Caribbean for three weeks spanning late November and early December. We had a little bit of rain in Curaçao, Barbados, Grenada, and Martinique, but the showers were always brief and gentle.

That wasn’t the case in Dominica. Here, the rain came down in sheets and lasted for hours.

On our second full day, it was pouring so hard that we only left our cottage to eat and get more groceries, and spent the rest of the time doing laundry and catching up on our inboxes.

The day wasn’t a loss, though — we got some delicious shawarmas for lunch at a place called Kenan Shawarma King, and spent our meal cuddling a tiny calico kitten. After lunch, we bought a big bag of kitten food for the owner, who was delighted.

As it continued to rain over the next few days, I realized that our clothes weren’t drying. We were hanging them on a drying rack inside, and they were still damp days later.

And it’s not like I was washing jeans — I brought a wardrobe almost entirely made of thin performance merino wool, which usually dries in less than half a day. How do people even dry their clothes here?!

Dry season in Dominica is technically from December to May, but rain can happen anytime. We soon learned that it would pour throughout our trip.

Exploring the Rainforests of Dominica

On our third full day, we decided to explore the interior of Dominica and spend thenight in Wotten Waven, a town known for its geothermal activity.

Even though Wotten Waven was only an hour and 15 minutes from Portsmouth according to Google Maps, we figured it would be safer to stay over, rather than rushing to get back before dark.

As we drove southward toward Roseau, the road changed. The closer we got to the city, the wider and smoother the roads became.

Of course, it wasn’t without its challenges. Google Maps sent us down a few dead ends until we finally made it to the Emerald Pool in UNESCO World Heritage-listed Morne Trois Pitons National Park.

We parked nearby, spent about 15 minutes walking through the forest, and made our way down a staircase to the pool.

This is the kind of place that makes you appreciate Dominica — the lush, thick vegetation, rivers, and waterfalls. It feels like the jungle setting was turned up to eleven.

It was a beautiful place to visit — but not a place where you necessarily need to linger, unless you want to swim. We took our photos, enjoyed the atmosphere, and climbed back up.

The good thing is that we set out early and were able to beat the cruise ship excursions. Had we gone in mid-afternoon, our photos would have been full of bobbing heads.

Hiking to Middleham Falls

After grabbing lunch at another roadside restaurant (with yet another cat, of course), Charlie and I drove to the trailhead for Middleham Falls. While the Emerald Pool and Middleham Falls look close on a map, you actually have to drive all the way back to the west coast, then down another inland road.

We chose Middleham Falls for our hike in Dominica because we wanted a hike that was around medium difficulty and not more than a few hours, with a great visual payoff. It was also fairly close to our final destination of the day, Wotten Waven.

The road to the trailhead was the single worst road we experienced in Dominica. This was a dirt road so badly torn up that you had to creep along at a snail’s pace or risk popping your tires.

But it wasn’t a very long drive to the trailhead, and soon we were in the parking lot, looking at the wreckage of a half-built eco-resort with grass roofs that had been abandoned mid-construction.

The hike to Middleham Falls is an out-and-back hike that is 5.3 km or 3.3 miles total and takes about 1.5-2 hours.

The hike started nicely, and soon the rain began to fall again. We didn’t mind it that much; we could handle it. Even when we passed a shaded gazebo that marked the halfway point, we didn’t feel the need to stop.

As we continued along dirt paths in the forest, climbing stairs into the hills, and stepping around giant tree roots, we breathed in that delicious forest air. The rain fell harder and harder, but the scent of the forest made me feel alive.

And there we were, probably a five-minute walk from the gorgeous waterfall, so close that we could hear the rush of water, and the trail…turned into a pile of rocks.

We would need to scramble on our hands and knees and climb down the boulders in order to get to the waterfall.

What the hell?!

The hike had been perfectly moderate until then, and nothing I’d read had mentioned scrambling.

We stood there, underneath our umbrellas, wondering if it was worth the risk. We would probably be fine. Or it could go very, very badly. And I did NOT want to risk hitting my head or breaking a bone in Dominica.

So we made the decision to call it. Five minutes from the waterfall. Oh well.

We hiked back to the gazebo at the halfway point to wait out the rain. The rain did not change whatsoever, and so we continued in the downpour.

Back at the car, I peeled off my soaked merino socks and squeezed out my hair. It was time to head to the hot springs.

Overall, Charlie and I thought this was a lovely hike until the end, and if it hadn’t been raining so hard, we would have tackled the scramble. But boulders plus sheets of rain was just too much.

Wotten Waven Hot Springs and Ti Kwen Glo Cho

There are lots of “hot springs resorts” in the town of Wotten Waven, but Ti Kwen Glo Cho is one that came highly recommended to me. It’s a popular spot for cruise ship excursions during the day, but if you stay overnight, you can enjoy the pools without the crowds.

Wotten Waven is perched on a hill in the interior of the island, with lots of colorful houses and churches. We found Ti Kwen Glo Cho easily, checked in, and were given a simple, rustic room with bunk beds that could have accommodated a family with kids.

The grounds at the resort are beautiful, filled with flowers, fruit trees, and nicely manicured paths. From the check-in area, you walk down staircases built into the hills until you reach the pools.

There are two pools — a “warm pool” and a “mud pool,” though to be honest they looked and felt the same — as well as a bathtub with a stream of water falling into it. A river flows behind the pools, and there’s a shaded changing area.

And while it was still raining, it felt absolutely divine slipping into that velvety warm water, surrounded by flowers as little cold raindrops dotted my cheeks. What a treat for sore muscles. By the late afternoon, we were two of only five people at the pools.

We did have one snafu — we went to the restaurant for dinner and the staff were annoyed that we hadn’t told them we wanted dinner when we checked in. That was our mistake.

If you want dinner, tell them when you check in. (They still fed us, and we had some delicious quesadillas.)

Something to keep in mind is that the walls are thin here. Staying in the room next to us was a family with two rambunctious kids, and just down the street was a Pentecostal church blasting its service.

Earplugs are always a smart thing to pack, wherever you travel, and that’s especially true for Ti Kwen Glo Cho.

A day visit at Ti Kwen Glo Cho costs $10 USD as of 2026, and double rooms with spa access start at $80 USD per night. Breakfast is $15 USD extra.

One thing I especially enjoyed is that Ti Kwen Glo Cho is owned by a local Dominican family. If you want to keep your money in local hands, this is a great place to do so.

A Day at the InterContinental

The next morning, Charlie and I took a final soak in the hot pools, had a tasty breakfast of eggs, beans, and plantains, and drove back to Portsmouth without incident.

And we decided to splurge.

By this time, we were tired of white-knuckling the terrible roads. Tired of being wet all the time. Tired of climbing stairs to get anywhere.

So we called the InterContinental and ordered day passes for the next day, at $37 USD each.

As we drove up that long driveway, I felt a bit embarrassed. Did I really travel to one of the least touristy places in the Caribbean, just to escape to a luxury resort? I roll my eyes at that kind of traveler.

And let’s talk about the most important part: it’s not like most Dominicans can pick up and spend the day at a luxury hotel when they need a break from their island. It’s not like they can decamp to a resort after a hurricane destroys their home.

That being said — luxury resorts, especially large resorts run by international chains like the InterContinental, are instrumental in growing Dominica’s tourism industry.

Yes, they employ locals, but they are also training locals in international hospitality standards. That training is critical to growing locally owned tourism in developing parts of the world.

I believe that many Dominican InterContinental employees will go on to open their own hotels and tourism businesses, and they’ll be better, more sustainable businesses as a result.

The InterContinental is perched on the coast, but there are no beaches. Instead, the pools feel a bit like the sea — you walk in and they deepen gradually.

And after the last several days, it was SO nice to sit on a lounger, read my Kindle, drink a coffee frappe, swim, and dry myself with a towel that was fluffy and not crispy, while enjoying the T-Pain-filled 2000s R&B playlist the resort was playing.

As usual, it rained hard for about 90 minutes. We spent that time in the restaurant. But this time, the sun actually came out afterward.

And those few hours of relaxation were exactly what we needed for the journey ahead.

Advance registration is required for day passes at the InterContinental Dominica Cabrits Resort & Spa. You can email info.dominica@ihg.com or call +1 767-445-1000. Passes are $37 USD on weekdays and $60 USD on weekends.

The Departure from Hell

Shortly before arriving in Dominica, we were notified that our WinAir flight from Dominica to St. Maarten had been rescheduled from 11:55 AM to 7:15 AM.

That threw a wrench into things — in order to make our flight, we would either need to leave Portsmouth in the middle of the night, or spend our final night by the airport.

I immediately vetoed driving on those roads after dark again, so we decided to shorten our stay at Kootney Resorts and drive to the town of Marigot while it was still light out the day before our departure.

At first I assumed we’d just stay at the airport hotel, but no, there was no airport hotel. There were actually no hotels near the airport. Just guesthouses.

No problem. We’d stay at a guesthouse. We booked the Golden Inn.

The drive back from Portsmouth to Marigot was terrifying once again, but I concentrated on breathing deeply through my fear, and I even managed to get a few photos.

We pulled up to the Golden Inn and nobody was home except a little boy around 10 years old, who showed us to a room reeking of old shrimp with a dirty unmade bed.

“Is your mom going to be home soon?” I asked him. He shrugged.

“Okay. We’ll get some food and come back and talk to your mom, okay?”

“Okay.”

And off we set to find some dinner in the town of Marigot. Google Maps had a handful of restaurants on the map.

We headed to the first one, La Petite Bistro. It had been shuttered for a long time.

We headed to the next one, JU-C FRU-T SMOOTH-E HUT. Also shuttered.

We drove to the Last Flight Bar & Grill. It had an airplane sitting next to it, but the restaurant was just a shell.

“Let’s just find a minimart or something,” I told Charlie. “We can eat chips and cookies for dinner if we have to.”

There were no minimarts, no grocery stores, no convenience stores. We started pulling over and asking locals if there was a restaurant, a store, anywhere we could buy food. And each time, they would say, “Not here,” and shrug.

Desperate, I hopped back into the car after my latest fruitless inquiry with a shop owner. “Let’s just go to the airport,” I told Charlie. “There HAS to be something there.”

We drove to the airport — and THERE WAS AN OPEN RESTAURANT! It was 5:50 PM, they were closing in ten minutes, and all they had left were sandwiches and fries.

We returned to the Golden Inn, where the owner was now home and had made up a clean bed for us. The shrimp smell was still terrible, but by that point, we weren’t going anywhere else.

And by then, we were expecting to just get out of Dominica with no further issues, but no, there was one more surprise planned to send us off! Our luggage was too heavy, the WinAir worker told us, and we would need to pay more.

“Fine,” I said. “I don’t care. We’ll pay.”

“And the machine isn’t working,” she said. “We can only take cash.”

“FINE,” I said through gritted teeth. “I will go to the ATM.” I would have paid whatever they asked.

As our flight took off, cresting over the hills of Dominica, I squeezed Charlie’s hand and sighed with relief. I have never been so relieved to leave an island.

What I Would Have Done Differently

So, if you’re reading this and you’d be interested in visiting Dominica, but doing it in a much better way than I did, that’s great!

Let me tell you what I would have done differently.

I would not have rented a car. I would have hired drivers. Even though Charlie drove well in Dominica, the scary drives turned me into a basket case, which is not how anyone should spend their vacation.

I would have stayed in the Roseau area for at least some of the time. Roseau is the most developed part of the island, with much better roads, the greatest variety of accommodation and restaurants, and most tours depart from here (though they’re primarily designed for cruise ship excursions).

While I enjoyed Portsmouth and especially staying at Kootney Resorts, I think it would be better suited for a shorter duration.

When I found out about the flight being rescheduled to early in the morning, I would have hired a driver to take us VERY early in the morning. It was absolutely not worth spending a night in Marigot.

I would have visited during the driest months of the year. While the dry season in Dominica technically runs from December to May, the driest months are February, March, and April.

I would not have trusted Google Maps, especially for restaurants. So many of the restaurants listed as active and open on Google Maps had been closed for months. I don’t know if this would have helped, but it would have kept my expectations in check.

I would have considered taking the ferry to Roseau rather than flying in. There is a passenger ferry called the FRS Express des Îles that runs from Guadeloupe to Dominica to Martinique to St. Lucia. While that didn’t work for our particular trip, this is a great way to avoid the airport altogether.

I would have packed backup protein bars. I always pack protein bars when traveling solo, and eat them when I arrive late or don’t feel like going out, but I don’t when traveling with Charlie, as he would NOT be happy eating a protein bar for dinner. But they would have saved us on the final night.

Is Dominica worth visiting?

Overall, I feel like Dominica is worth visiting if you’re a certain kind of traveler — the kind of traveler who genuinely enjoys visiting less developed places and relishes the challenges of travel.

(And no, I’m not talking about the people who THINK they should enjoy visiting less developed places — I mean people who genuinely prefer them.)

Dominica is also a nice choice for people interested in outdoor exploration and hiking, especially hardcore hiking, but not beaches.

But you need to be both of these things: an outdoorsy person AND a person who enjoys the challenges of less developed countries. If I were traveling for outdoor exploration and hiking, I’d visit Costa Rica or Guatemala in a heartbeat before returning to Dominica, because they have much better travel infrastructure.

Additionally, if you’re visiting Dominica, you need to be okay with a LOT of rain, including rain while hiking, swimming, and hot spring-basking.

My friend’s parents owned a house in Dominica for many years, until Hurricane Maria destroyed it. Her dad is the kind of person who enjoys being on a tropical island, far away from everyone, ESPECIALLY tourists.

Back in 2022, Charlie and I happened to be in Puerto Vallarta when our friend’s dad passed through for one night after a vacation on the Oaxaca coast. We met up, and Charlie asked him how he liked Vallarta.

“I’M NEVER COMING HERE AGAIN!” he yelled.

For him, Dominica was perfect. (“He would still be there if he weren’t 78 years old,” my friend told me.)

Would I go back to Dominica? To be completely honest, I don’t see the need to return. But not in a “I would NEVER go back!” way.

There are so many Caribbean islands I would rather return to than Dominica (Bequia, Curaçao, Martinique, and St. Lucia, among others). Not to mention the Caribbean islands I haven’t visited yet (Anguilla is hopefully next).

Our time on this planet is limited. I’d rather spend my time exploring places I want to see, not returning to a place I didn’t love just to make a point.

I feel like I’ve given Dominica a chance, and even though the trip was challenging, I still had some moments of joy, like the Indian River trip, most of the hike to Middleham Falls, and our time at Wotten Waven.

Dominica is not the place for me. But it might be the place for you.

Does Dominica sound like your kind of place?

The post Is Dominica Worth Visiting? (Don’t make the mistakes I made!) appeared first on Adventurous Kate.
